text:
Great video! I've been rolling bjj for 3 months now. I'm located at a great gym with a great culture, with the head coach from America. Unfortunately, I got ringworm after a few weeks of training. I took my hygiene seriously, but I have started to shower at my gym to prevent catching staff/ringworm ect.

What I took away from this video / linking to my own training:

This question was asked to the wrong guy. You need to ask a guy in his late 40's, 50's or older. In my 50's now and I can say that I had a great time training in martial arts (judo, karate, jiujitsu, boxing and MMA). In my 40's I realized I was having problems, too much wear and tear on the body (mostly my neck and shoulders but also my hands and knees). Eventually I made the decision to stop training as the injuries were coming more frequently and taking much longer to heal, while at the same time I was slowing down with reflex time. Now, I miss training. There is nothing like training and going toe to toe with someone, testing yourself in so many ways. Having also worked in security and law enforcement on two continents, I can also say that having martial arts knowledge did save me from at least getting seriously injured more than once in real world situations. All of this said, was it worth it? Probably not. That doesn't stop me from feeling this void of not rolling these days. I think the advice I'd give someone is to train, but to train in moderation. Had we continued going hard every time, it would have been much more injurious. Recently, I've been training with a guy from another dojo that's more BJJ-focused and the increase in close calls on my part is very noticeable. And I hate it. I just want to have fun, learn and go home uninjured, sometimes I have work right after training and when I don't, my boss still relies on me for the next day and I just hate getting injured as well. And what were these close calls caused by? Going hard, i.e. pulling joint locks fast. Trying to execute dangerous moves, especially takedowns targeting the knees with a sideways motion or turning me around on the ground by rapidly applying an arm lock targeting the shoulder. Not trusting me not to hurt him, and applying painful and at times dangerous counters to stop me from what I wasn't intending on doing in the first place. Did any of those situations need to be as dangerous as they were? Nope. And especially the last one, this culture of not trusting, is not something I want to see poisoning the dojo I train at. We all go onto the mat knowing that the other person cares about our wellbeing and this trust is what enables learning because fighting or hard rolling is not where you learn the best. Your brain is in an adrenaline-filled response, unable to think clearly. It surely is beneficial to put your brain into such a situation every once in a while, but for regular training, going slow and allowing your partner to do stuff and learn is best.

text:
I trained BJJ for over a year before I joined the USMC and earned a Blue Belt. The Marines have something called MCMAP (Marine Corps Martial Arts Program). Out of boot camp all Marines earn a Tan Belt (entry level belt). When I got to my first unit the MCMAP instructor was a Brown Belt. He was blown away that I was able to land 'advanced techniques' like triangle chokes, keylocks, and armbar variations. His head exploeded the first time I pulled Rubber Guard (Eddie Bravo had recently gained a lot of popularity and had published his Jiu Jitsu Unleashed book). They acted like I was some kind of grappling prodigy. I wasn't, I was just an average Blue Belt at my local BJJ gym. I was pretty shocked to see how little some of the more advanced MCMAP techniques were things I saw kids learning in BJJ classes. 

When I got my Black Belt in MCMAP, the instructors routinely would ask me for tips on how to use techniques in different situations. I would end up helping teach the classes and it actually had an impact on many of my fellow students. I loved when I had wrestlers working with me. We would feed off of each other on the mats and I think we all ended up elevating our game. By the time I was in class to get my Black Belt I had become much more familiar with my Rubber Guard and was usually trying to work on those techniques. I remember throwing an Oma Plata one day and the entire class stopped and it convinced several people to start training BJJ on the side. 

My son (age 9) recently started training and after his first day of classes told me that he can't wait to learn more!

text:
The first time I was invited to train jiu jitsu I was 21 or 22. I absolutely loved it and was consistent for 6ish months and even did a local comp 12 weeks in. I did horrible but it was awesome 😂 After that, I didn’t train again for over a year. And that was the beginning of a cycle that perpetuated for years. 1-3 months on, a year off. On repeat.  

Fast forward to now, I’m 32, married with 2 kids and the guys that originally invited me are all black belts and brown belts. 

For the last 5/6 months, I’ve gotten real serious about making bjj more of a lifestyle routine. Just a week ago I competed in my first no-gi comp. I didn’t win that one either but I certainly did a lot better this time 🤣

If there’s anything I regret about my journey so  far, it’s that I didn’t stick with it 10 years ago. Not because of the belts. But because of the lack of progress as a man that I missed out on from not making it a financial or physical priority. I got fat, I became stagnant, I got lazy. I literally couldn’t carry my kids upstairs without getting winded.  All because I made excuses to not train or take care of myself. Look, I get it. I’ve got a job, wife, 2 toddlers and a mortgage to pay. We’re all busy. I only train 2 times a week on average. Occasionally I’ll get to a 3rd practice, but that’s rare. Do what you can and commit to what’s reasonable within the non-negotiables of your schedule. 
 
Of course the physical perks of getting in shape are awesome. And training is a ton of fun. But the best part of all, it’s helping me be a better father and husband by instilling discipline and focus in my daily routine that didn’t exist before.

And look, I don’t want to make the sport seem like it’s something it’s not, but it truly has given me a confidence and drive that I had lost years ago.  I can carry my kids up a flight of stairs without losing my breath. I can rough house with them and throw them across the couch almost endlessly 😂 I have more clarity. My stress levels have dramatically lessened. I feel regulated emotionally. And this clarity has allowed me to be more present, focused and supportive of my wife on a daily basis. 

It hasn’t been this crazy spiritual revelation that some people often try to make it. Get to a local church and read the bible for that. But the mental clarity and physical improvements have been life changing for my family. 

This has turned into a novel. Didn’t intend to do that, haha. As I listened to the video, I felt compelled to share the journey I’ve been on in hopes that someone who may be in a similar spot would see this and be encouraged to commit to training something. Make the commitment. Even if it’s not bjj. Maybe it’s running or weight lifting. It doesn’t matter. At some point you will look back and you will regret not making the commitment. God Bless ✌️

text:
I’d put it slightly differently. It may be worth doing anyway, but if you don’t enjoy it you ain’t gonna. But the fact that you didn’t love it as a kid don’t mean you’re sure to hate it as an adult. You were a child and thought as children think.

Here’s what I think might have been going on. You weren’t a naturally athletic kid. Strong, fast, coordinated, those kind of things. So as a beginner, you double sucked, from a combination of physical and skill reasons. And, also as a kid, you needed to be good to feel validated and enjoy the thing. Instead you got non-stop demonstrations of being not good , or not as as good as the other kids.

But you’re older now. It’s possible that you could go to a bjj club and enjoy the process of learning, instead of chasing the validation of “being awesome”. As an adult you might see that pretty much everyone who comes to bjj suck at it for a long time. Accepting failure and learning from it is central to the art. Accepting that there are people whom you can beat easily (very few at first), people on about your level, and people who are so far beyond you that you can’t even imagine giving them a challenging roll. That’s an important aspect of bjj. But you don’t need to compete with them, in fact, you shouldn’t. The person you’re trying to beat is yourself from last month.

I’m 54. I’ve been doing this for less than two years. There are old blackbelts whom I will never catch up with, in the decades I have left. There are 25-year-olds with competition ready bodies who could fold me in half even if they wasn’t five or ten years ahead of me in skill. But myself from last spring… I’d smash that guy.

So give it a try. You might find that some things that felt intolerable to you then are insignificant now. You might find things to love that you were blind to back then. They are there.

Cheers

My kids learn Muay Thai and western boxing for striking, wrestling and jiujitsu for ground confidence, and judo for transitioning between the two. We don’t emphasize anything high level. Just master four basic principles of each martial art. I really mean master it. 
Must Thai: perfect punch, elbow, knee, and kicking technique.
Wrestling/Jiujitsu: chokes, arm/leg locks/bars, take down offense and defense. 
Judo: four basic throws. 
It’s for self defense not competition in our house. 
If they want to compete they can lick a discipline and go for it, but regardless everyone has to MASTER those basic things in those specific disciplines. 
I subscribe to the idea that I’d more fear the person that has practiced a single move a thousand times, than a hundred moves one time.
I enjoy judo the best at my age now. When I was younger I preferred striking.

Started BJJ in November. I haven't full rolled yet, other than little spurts while practicing techniques. My partner is also a white belt. One day our normal prof wasn't there so a brown belt taught the class. 

We asked him for help on a technique that was just passing guard into side control (I'm horrible with the names). So he did the technique on me, and the difference in pressure/weight/uncomfort with how he did it vs how me and my partner were doing it was unreal. I mean it was a quick pass, but it was like he had so much weight that just transitioned from my leg, up through my hip, to my midsection making it hard to breath.

Joe's line about how most people have no idea how defenseless they'd be if a BJJ black belt grabbed ahold of them makes me think of that small exchange. If you just watched it, you'd see nothing different, but BJJ is so deep. It's "simple" sure, "you grab this sleeve, this collar, foot here, pull/twist and now you're on top"... but there's so many small things with weight, momentum, the grip you make when you grab, shifting weight a little bit here at this moment, etc and it just completely changes how effective/smooth it feels. It's nuts. And addictive.

People from other arts endlessly malign the BJJ guard, and while it obviously is not a very practical or recommendable strategy to pull guard in MMA or self defense the majority of the time, it is still well within the realm of possibility that you will trip and fall, be taken down, be attacked while sitting down, or countless other such scenarios. A lot of the time, standing up may be a superior option to entering a confrontation on those terms, but that is not guaranteed to be either possible or ideal. 
 For this reason, I think it is good that despite the stigma, there are people in BJJ who spend so much time developing and exhibiting strategies which begin from open guard. It is not a comprehensive self-preservation strategy, but it's usefulness as a skill depends as much on the circumstances of the confrontation as it does with striking, wrestling, running, shooting or parkour.

text:
I came to BJJ at 29 y.o. With almost no previous experience in martial art. I've never been in a fight since high school, and I never been good at any of them either. I really don't know how to act in fights.

But eventually I started BJJ, and I see many debates on it's effectiveness, comparing to Boxing or other standing martial arts. And most of the people talking about it in the extremes. But for average people like myself... whether it BJJ, grapling, boxing, muy tai or etc... it's already an important edge against average agressor in a street fight.

Why I personally choose BJJ, because it have grappling base, and after first trainings you understand how much you're not feeling your body, how much untrained person is not in control, not even avare of his body. And BJJ helps me be in my body, feel all my muscles, control it. And that what really might be helpful.

Second thing is that it really teaches you to think strategicly, think of every move, yes most of the time you think in terms of BJJ rules, but the idea and habit of calmly think of the next most effective move easily can be applied in a street fight too. In life generally!

And the third, IMHO BJJ is much more sustainable martial art against Boxing or raw grappling in a perspective: when you are a middle aged man, have family, bussiness, kids... you don't necessarily prioritize being champion, you don't have such body recovering ability as young guys, but you want to be strong, you want to be able to fight. And BJJ alows you to do so even when you get old. Yes if you are young, you can easily be explosive and agressive BJJ fighter, but you can be still competitive and effective in BJJ even when you not. I believe in many other martial arts you have  a much less time to do this sports effectively, and after that you will be getting more injures and less fun, than actually training and improving.

But that's just my perspective.

Martial arts will absolutely work in the street, if you train them with proper intent. If you are a sport grappler, then the video is right, a street fight probably won't go well for you. If you train whatever style you are learning with intent to protect yourself, then you will likely be fine. Of course, there are no guarantees, but based on my experience, this statement is true. 

BJJ as commonly taught today, is not conducive to a real world situation, because it primarily only focuses on the ground fighting techniques... you know, literally the last place you want to be in the real world. While that is good to know, it is more than likely that you will respond based on how you train, and typically at the lowest level of your training. So get out there and train with intent, and bring back what martial arts were for, being martial.

text: In my late 50s now and can speak with a great deal of personal experience having been in many street fights, bar brawls, etc. Also, very experienced in what I consider the best base a person can have for self defense at the time I trained. Before I list them I want to make it clear, there is a HUGE difference in self-defense and prepared fighting. When two people are prepared to fight one another there no longer exist an element of surprise. The element of surprise is a big plus. Self-defense is based on surprise and trying everything possible to actually avoid conflicts, and in almost all cases anyone who is highly trained usually embraces the practice of avoiding conflicts. With all that said, this is what I was successful in and trained heavily in for many years. Folkstyle wrestling, boxing, WKA Kickboxing (not US PKA), and a touch of JKD (wasn't much of that around in 80s). Training in all these styles one of the best things I learned was proper distance and timing, you'll be surprised how effective just not getting hit or being taken down can be🤣. The other thing is you gain a sense of calm, if you're constantly training in combat with other high level people a street confrontation doesn't concern you, unless you're confronted by multiple attackers and you're by yourself. Bit older now and would like to try some BJJ, that wasn't around when I was younger. One last thing I will say that makes a big difference is one's will. So whatever you train in, train hard, and try to avoid confrontations. But if the confrontation cannot be avoided, believe in yourself, don't give up, and if you overwhelm your attacker don't over do it.

text:
It great to see Tony Jeffries experiencing something new and sharing his experiences from the perspective of a beginner.  

It's also refreshing to hear a YouTube influencer with professional fighting experience state that, yes, training does count towards being able to defend yourself.  It has become the trend for some influential  martial arts YouTubers to totally dismiss sport fighting and martial arts - even the pragmatic ones like MMA, boxing, and BJJ calling them sports and ill equipped for actual self-defence.  In fact, one well known martial arts YouTuber, who is a former professional MMA fighter, who I respect, boldly states: "Most martial artists don't know how to fight."  I do agree that some fighting arts are more suited to give you self-defence skills while others are not. 

That said, I would say that both boxing and BJJ (or other grappling art) are useful for self-defence for different purposes.   

Boxing (as well as kickboxing, and muay Thai) not only teaches you how to strike a moving target and evading strikes, but it also trains you the conditioning to absorb hits.  No one wants to take a hit, not even in a light semi-contact spar, but boxing (and kickboxing, muay Thai, and some of the harder karate styles) will train that mental focus to not fold under pressure of getting punched.  This is where untrained fighters fall apart is when they get hit for real the first time and go into a confused state of shock and panic -- especially if you get cut or bleed.  

There is that argument that you want to stay on your feet in a self-defence situation because there might be multiple attackers although I think that's often overblown because most attacks - unless you frequent rough bars or neighborhoods - are probably more 1-on-1 like a road rage incident, or some street person with mental health issues attacking you.  

The one valid argument for not taking someone to the ground is that there are no comfy mats on the street to fall on.  Example: during an MMA class I was taking one time we were doing take take down drills.   I was a three striped BJJ blue belt at the time and my opponent for the shark tank drill was a beginner.  I easily got a single leg but my head was out of position to his outside and he instinctively guillotined my head by instinct as I drove him to the mat and my head got spiked ("DDT" in professional wrestling circles).  While I was okay due to the mat and my excessively hard head the situation may have been a different outcome if it were on concrete.

Now although one can argue that you can do a safer standing throw like a seoi nage, uchi-mata, or kosoto gari, you are unlikely to use those techniques due to their low probability unless you are a black belt in judo.  As a BJJ guy you are unlikely to be really, really good at those throws especially because the first two expose your back so you're unlikely to train them regularly and so a typical BJJ guy is unlikely to be as well versed with standing throws as a judo brown or black belt especially since the attacker is unlikely to be wearing a do-gi.  The BJJ bread and butter is likely to be a double leg, and single leg and those moves entail some risk because you are driving the opponent to the ground and going with him on to hard concrete.

However BJJ is relevant if the conditions are right, and especially if the attacker happens to be wearing a Golden Gloves Champion T-shirt!  BJJ has it's benefits against a single attacker; especially if they are more aggressive than you.  If you can clinch up and even take them to the ground they are unlikely to be able to throw any kind of meaningful punches.  BJJ is also a more humane way of dealing with a single attacker as video footage of Ryan Hall, and Matt Serra subduing aggressors in a restaurant and holding them -- again, evidence that many attacks in daily life are likely to be 1-on-1 than the worst case multiple attackers in a bar scenario -- unless you happen to be in a bar.   Also, what if you're getting overwhelmed by punches?  What do MMA fighters automatically do when they are getting overwhelmed with punches -- they will go for a double leg or other takedown to try and survive.

The one argument I use against those you say that ground grappling is pointless for street self-defence because they would never take the fight to the ground is: what if you get taken to the ground?  Every punk who watches UFC has seen a double-leg and probably tried it on a friend while roughhousing.  If you get taken to the ground do you know how to escape?  Do you know how to bridge escape if you get mounted?  Do you know how to do a technical standup so you don't get kicked in the face while scrambling up?

One martial art that has not been mentioned as very good for self-defence is muay Thai.  Muay Thai addresses multiple ranges.  Although it lacks the ground game, it addresses kicking range, punching range, knee and elbow range, and clinching range.  It has the strikes using 8 limbs, it has the conditioning to keep you physically fit, it has taken clinching and elevated it to a specialized set of skills, and has very effective trips throws from the clinch and you do not need sleeves or lapels to do them. 

But if I had to choose between boxing and BJJ for street self-defence...hmmmmm...tough choice because they are both important.  But for me I'm going to say BJJ specifically designed for self-defence (e.g. Gracie Combatives).  No fancy worm guards, no lasso grips or berimbolos,...just dealing with an aggressive unskilled attacker throwing haymakers.

Of course, there's the other option: stay out of trouble, don't piss other people off, learn to keep the ego in check and walk away...run if you must because a street attack is no about winning; it's about making sure no one gets seriously hurt especially you.

Getting your opponent to the ground with the hope of securing an armbar, triangle or RNC  will get you injured before you do any damage to your adversary due to the surface you are fighting on.

In the ring or on the mat is a different story, where a grappling art will likely prevail most of the time.

text: One thing about the ground that I believe goes unmentioned many times is that if you end up on the ground it could be because you were already tackled, kicked or hit or taken down in such a way that you broke something and can no longer defend yourself effectively on the ground even if you know jiu-jitsu. So even for a jiu-jitsu practitioner he may be in a disadvantageous situation by the time he is on the ground; he could twist something in the clinch as well. Boxing helps to get away from the situation before an injury leading the person to the ground happens. Also what most people today seem to not discuss very much is the clinch where a lot of grappling happens and which is the transitional range between boxing and the ground. If the defender in the clinch has judo or other clinch grappling skill he might be relatively comfortable in that range where the opponent presumably believed himself to be superior, probably based on his size. So even in a grappling scenario the ground does not just happen right away when the boxing range is closed but rather the situation must first pass through the clinch unless one person was tackled or knocked down by a strike.

There is a reason why grappling is the oldest and more prevalent martial art across cultures AND history. Isometric holding and grabbing is a more "primal" movement, think what babies do. Boxing is good. But don't focus on a boxing match. You aren't going in the ring. Instead, be able to land a hook (right or left) when both your hands are low and you're standing a little sideways but not much, while an angry person is giving you the business.  The fastest punch you can land is your right or left hook. No wind up necessary. It's the closest to him. He will not even see it.  On the bag, or a dummy, practice that combo:  for me,  a south paw; right foot a tad forward, I'll do right hook, a looping left,  and a right cross. No straight punches. You aren't fighting Evander Holyfield, trying to get between his guard. They are loopers on the chin, jaw, to torque his head and end it as fast as possible.

When it comes to doing it thousands and thousands of times, don't worry about technique. You want those punches to be solid and thudding, using your trunk to turn, but don't even focus on that. When you do exercises like that, making sure the shots are 1) hard at the point of impact and 2) fast, your  body will optimize this for you. It takes time.

text:
A few related tips from my personal experience to help my man:
First, and this is related to what he mentioned about mental training. I was a competitive boxer when I was younger, and I noticed that every time I would have a boxing match, I was nervous, but as soon as the actual fight stared, it (the fear) would disappear. So, I decided to harness this same reaction to work to my advantage in the street. Mentally, I would go over and over in my mind that I’m going to feel fear, it’s normal, and I accept it. After that was firmly established, I then repeatedly told myself that as soon as I feel fear, I attack. In other words, I trained my mind to use the feeling of fear itself as a trigger to attack. Most people don’t prepare themselves to deal with fear, so once they get in a legit dangerous situation, they become overwhelmed. The feeling of fear one faces in the ring is much different than the fear felt when in serious danger of losing one’s life or getting badly hurt. In such a situation, the best thing to do is preemptively strike, but many people freeze and/or panic, and that  reaction is not beneficial. However,  if you tell yourself over and over something along the lines of “if I have no choice but to defend myself, that means my only option is to fight, and the accompanying fear is my signal to attack.” Now, it is very important to attack within the first few seconds of the fear hitting. If you train this regularly, you are essentially training your body to react to the feeling of fear before you mind has a chance to start thinking. 
The above training, along with regular sparring and power training will give you confidence in your ability to defend against attacks and finish a fight.

text:
🔴🔴🔴Compared to boxing, MMA often acts as a refuge for those who are not good at real fistfights and lack the courage to face their opponent in a clean stance.

Why is MMA criticized as a "sport for incompetent boxers":

Lack of boxing technique: Most MMA fighters have a loose stance and chaotic punches without a hint of elegance. Instead of technical mastery, they rely on somehow "making" their opponent "feel good" because they wouldn't survive the first round in the ring with their fists.

Choking as a sign of weakness: Khabib's win over McGregor is a perfect example of this sporting wretchedness. Khabib didn't do anything special, he didn't show any dominant sportsmanship, he just hung on to his opponent and held him until he started to tear him apart. When someone can't knock out an opponent like a man with an honest punch, they resort to this primitive hugging. It's just a desperate attempt to avoid a real fight.

Misery instead of strength: Choking is the height of embarrassment in professional sports. It seems more like the attack of aggressive lunatics on the street than the performance of a top athlete. The fact that MMA rules allow something like this only proves that this "sport" has resigned itself to any aesthetics and honor.

Killing the viewing experience: Nothing ruins a sports broadcast more than two guys rolling around on the ground in some weird knot for ten minutes. It's boring, visually off-putting, and it completely lacks the dynamism that boxing has. The viewer wants to see power and precision, not someone crawling around on the ground looking for their opponent's neck.

Conclusion: Boxing is about character and facing your opponent head-on, knowing that your skill and toughness will decide. 

MMA is just a show of cowardly tactics, where instead of fighting, you run to the ground, which makes it a poor concoction of true sportsmanship.

text:
If you get in a ring and don’t know how to avoid any technique but for punches , you gonna learn real quick. All the arts use different ranges of engagement. A fighter that only ever got punched will not be very effective at a man who has been kicking and being kicked for years will be at a further range and closing the gap has dire consequences. Equally trained I give the mma guy the win every time
  This all hinges on how the martial artist has trained compared to the boxer. A kick boxer who has only used touch training and never really been hit will be destroyed by a boxer with minimal experience because they train real time real damage where a martial artist will usually be trained to pull the power of impact as to avoid damage all together. This type of training will not suffice. 

   Provided the martial artist had engaged in training with impact like the boxer, the boxer stands no chance when equally trained. A martial artist has so many more weapons and use a range the boxer can’t comprehend. Boxers have an about 6-10 fundamental strikes in his arsenal. 

A mixed martial artist has many, many more  start with 9 basic striking weapons that can be used in an unlimited variety of ways. Additionally, beyond the addition of knees, elbow, feet ( 5 or 6 possible kicks from infinite angles) and head butts the mixed arts have take downs. Locks and submissions, finger jabs to eyes, and so much more. Mixed fighters commonly train and fight in realms that aren’t even part of boxings thinking.  Boxers have absolutely no defenses,, counters, or ways to avoid take downs. Most boxers can’t recognize or have the tools to detect an attempted take down and have absolutely no ability to defend or strike when on the ground. Knock a boxer over and he’s pretty much reduced to being a human paper weight.

   While there are boxers who have experience in other arts and ranges of fighting, here I’m addressing the arts themselves not the subjective experience of a particular individual. Once a boxer trainings in another art he becomes a mixed martial artist. 

    I’ve never said boxing is inferior nor would I ever discourage the practice there of. In my personal opinion, boxing is absolutely the best way to train a man’s hands and body to deliver the most damaging punches of all the arts. 

   Fun fact, karate as an art has absorbed boxing thru fisticuffs long before the western world adopted the art. The basic karate stance where the left arm almost looks as if held in a front block like posture and the right hand chambered at the solar plexus is the exact same posture used in fisticuffs as seen on the fighting Irish team logo. 

    Quite a few martial arts have adopted boxing for obvious reasons.

Lack of boxing technique: Most MMA fighters have a loose stance and chaotic punches without a hint of elegance. Instead of technical mastery, they rely on somehow "making" their opponent "feel good" because they wouldn't survive the first round in the ring with their fists.

Choking as a sign of weakness: Khabib's win over McGregor is a perfect example of this sporting wretchedness. Misery instead of strength: Choking is the height of embarrassment in professional sports. It seems more like the attack of aggressive lunatics on the street than the performance of a top athlete. The fact that MMA rules allow something like this only proves that this "sport" has resigned itself to any aesthetics and honor.

Killing the viewing experience: Nothing ruins a sports broadcast more than two guys rolling around on the ground in some weird knot for ten minutes. It's boring, visually off-putting, and it completely lacks the dynamism that boxing has. The viewer wants to see power and precision, not someone crawling around on the ground looking for their opponent's neck.

Conclusion: Boxing is about character and facing your opponent head-on, knowing that your skill and toughness will decide.

text: There are a number of reasons boxing is more dangerous than ufc. A few off the top of my head are: 1) superior strikers, of course ufc has world class strikers, but they train more movements making boxers punches on average stronger. 2) focus on headshots, ufc has many ways of ending a fight. Boxing is ended by knockout and points. 3.) The 10 count is a huge problem in boxing. One knockout should end a fight. In boxing people sustain huge brain busting blows but recover within the 10 count only to recieve another. That can and has killed people. 4.) Paradoxically, boxing gloves are more dangerous than mma gloves., which are in turn more dangerous than bare knuckles. Extra padding a.) Allows the user to hit harder without injuring themselves and b,) delivers more concussive force to the brain by acting as a larger fulcrum. Cuts are not dangerous, hemotomas ond your skin are not dangerous, cranial hemotomas are life threatening. Keep in mind their are no nerves in the brain so your subjective opinion on mma gloves hurting more does not reflect the internal damage being done. All this boils down to the ufc is bloody and breaks bones, but boxing damages peoples brains waaaaay more.

What many fail to realize is that fighting is really a base set of skills and abilities completely independent from style, and that most styles work just fine when you can actually fight. That is why, for instance, karate is divided into kata and kumite etc.

Why karate doesn't work when kickboxing does:

Karate (shotokan), as well as taekwondo and kung fu are procedure-oriented martial arts. In karate training proper technique execution is the most important part of the training. Therefore no matter what is your age, sex, height, weight, general athleticism, strong points, weak points - everyone trains the same. Experimentation and creativity of adepts is often frowned upon and definitely not encouraged. Same warmup, same kihon and kata. Kumite is usually the last part of the class, and many schools neglect it heavily, for various reasons. Lack of safety gear, lack of a proper number of advanced enough students to do it safely, lack of a good number of instructors to ensure it's all going on without major injuries or other issues.
Sparring is the ultimate test (aside competition) of a combat ability, it's stress testing technique to ensure as much as possible that you can perform techniques in a real self defense situation. If you don't spar - you aren't a fighter. You can call yourself a martial artist but it doesn't mean much if you don't spar.

Kickboxing (Muay Thai included, also in boxing) is a result-oriented martial art. And the result is winning the fight. Aside fundamentals- technique isn't as important as long as you can keep winning. Individuality of fighters plays a much bigger role in training. Boxing has boxing styles that fit many different body types- larger and slower dudes can be sluggers or boxer-punchers, smaller dudes with bad reach can become infighters while fast footwork dudes with good reach can be outboxers. In muay thai you have like 5 common types of nak muay, some are better with kicks, others with punches etc. Experimentation and creativity of fighters is encouraged as long as it lets them win sparrings.
And yeah, sparrings. A lot of them, often including separate sparring hours, either as extra or so regular classes aren't 75% sparring.

This is why karate doesn't work, the issue is at the core. And when it works- it produces capable fighters 2-3 times slower than kickboxing. Often relying on the practitioner doing much more work in his "free" time to improve as a fighter.

And I mean shotokan. Kyokushin has a strong focus on kumite, full contact. Lots of injuries but it really produces hard hitting, durable mfs. Can't take a face punch for the life of them, but kyokushin is a great supplementary martial art for boxers who want to get their punching power to the next level. They also have few cool punches unseen in boxing classes, like "stabbing uppercuts" (don't know the name, sorry) or short straight punches from their wide guard, that pack a power between a jab and a straight.

Shotokan and taekwondo are still decent martial arts, about medium tier in usability, above stuff like aikido, ninjutsu, systema (yuck), wing chun (yuck), tai chi, capoeia, jeet kune do, most kung fu in general. And they make decent supplementary skillsets for boxers and kickboxers. Special mention for muay thai and taekwondo- those 2 make a wonderful, devastating combination.

Elements of karate work, however, many of these elements are also taught in other martial arts like kickboxing, which has less fluff and filler. Many elements of karate are also effectively a waste of time if your goal is to learn how to fight, which on some level is a pretty typical motivation for practicing martial arts. Take kata for instance this is effectively dancing. It is not shadow boxing because it is a preset arrangement of movements whereas shadow boxing is free form. Judo has kata as well, however, the difference is judo kata are short and each are obviously applicable to their practical use. Karate bunkai are typically one small step removed from larping and generally also involve massive modifications to how the technique is performed, so why not perform it that way without the partner as well? Because again it's just dancing. There are a small minority of techniques which both work and are also not included in other martial arts which makes things like karate worth researching but not directly practicing. Same for TKD, kung fu, etc similar.

I would be very grateful if you researched Bujinkan a bit. I found it to be the most well-balanced and useful martial art for myself, as it consists of countless elements that don't necessarily require physical strength, which is what I would most likely lose at anyway (although we do practice Bujinkan's variations of kicks and punches, and my all-time favorite will always be the "omote shutō", an edge-of-the-palm chop). It teaches me how to use an opponent's balance against themselves, how to fight efficiently with any object I can grab nearby, multiple ways to evade with some additional benefit... We have lengthy summer camps where we learn how to be sneaky, how to run away safely, how to use the environment to our advantage, how to climb and how to land with the least impact possible. We use various weapons in our trainings, including knives, swords, sticks of different lengths (hanbō, jo, bō), ropes, chains and etc. We know how to break bones or just make some lock/grab feel painful enough so the opponent is unwilling to continue (considering they are not drunk, of course...). We have some aikidō moves, but we inflict pain with them and don't really follow the way of peace aikidō preaches, although it's always in our hands how much pain we make the opponent endure. 
For multiple reasons this cannot be considered a sport or a competitive martial art, so we continue practicing it in the shadow haha...

The martial art originates from ninjutsu, an art far beyond what the media made it out to be. Maybe the ninja people could never create fire and lightning, but they surely adapted well to the nature around them and knew how to use it against the people who dared invade their sacred lands (who were mostly samurai with their legions, that's why ninjutsu also incorporated kendō and iaidō, ninja kinda stole the techniques from the people who attacked them lmao)

I myself practice Bujinkan overseas, in our local slavic dōjō, but I've even been lucky enough to attend a seminar in Japan, its motherland... 
Wish you all the best on your martial arts journey, and I hope my own journey bears fruit later when I'm more experienced (have been doing this for 3 years now, need to continue pushing).
Take care and let's grow together!

text:
I think much of this is very good food for thought but, by extension, kicking a knife out of somebody's hand probably won't work for most people most of the time, if we're really talking about playing the odds and not just saying that "there are no guarantees and so anything is possible with any technique". Playing the odds means prioritizing the perceived probability of outcomes over just the sheer possibility of outcomes even though both can be valid. As with the rear naked choke, all techniques aren't of equal value or utility just because someone somewhere has probably made virtually any technique work under some set of circumstances.

Rightly or wrongly, any set of techniques within any system of martial arts is an assessment of what probably will and won't work in combat, even though there are often surprises when various systems and their assumptions about combat collide. As just a practical matter, many people become best at countering fighters using their own style because that's what they are most familiar with, and train against, most often. In terms of time and resources, you have to train in something at the expense of not training in other things, even though as Bruce Lee famously pointed out, you also need to keep your mind open to other things that work and various systems can be too rigid in their combat assumptions.

To bring the thing full circle, how many instructors who were present and saw the knife kicked away twice would or wouldn't advise it to their students as a technique with a good probability of success? Saying it could never work obviously does go too far, but what is the probability of success for most people? If the answer is "nobody can say because there are just too many variables involved" - and this could be said of any technique - then there are no odds to play because there is no way to assess/calculate them to begin with.

If the knife defense instructor had said "that probably won't work in a real fight" instead of "you can't go kicking knives out of people's hands", would the instructor have been wrong?

Shotokan is all about precision and form, with lower stances, strong techniques, and a big focus on kata (forms) and kihon (basics). Sparring isn’t usually full-contact, so it’s more about discipline and technical skill.

Kyokushin, on the other hand, is full-on with conditioning and full-contact sparring. It’s known for developing mental and physical toughness with techniques designed for power and endurance.

Basically, Shotokan is precision and discipline, while Kyokushin is toughness and power!

If you wan to learn something for fun that’s fine, just be honest with what you’re learning it for, but don’t be fooled if you learn a martial art for self defense and the art doesn’t compete. You don’t have to compete but there needs to be a big enough of a pool of people who can test and prove the art actually works, if the art doesn’t compete full contact then it won’t work a lot of karate styles and nearly all Kung fu fall under this category. 

The reason people say if it doesn’t work in the  ring then it won’t work is because the ring, cage, mat, is where one can test and prove if a technique works or not, and if you can’t test it news flash it probably won’t work. You can apply some principles to some techniques  opening up your jab can turn into a nukite or adjust the hight of your front kick and boom there you have a groin shot; same with  a side kick to a joint kick. 

TMA guys need to quit coddling each other there are styles in martial art that work and don’t work and there are whole systems that don’t work. Sometimes it’s the practioners not sparing or competing (most of the time) and sometimes the art or style is completely useless (systema, ninjitsu, wing chun, tai chi, shorin ryu).

The real risk of sunk-cost fallacy means that if people start in a useless martial art they end up feeling stuck in it even after realising it’s a waste of time and money. After investing so much on the road to a black belt, they feel they need stick with it to at least say they’re a black belt.

If they start in a martial art without a belt system, like boxing or wrestling, there’s no such problem. They learn something useful, can quit at any time and won’t have lost anything as the focus the entire time is on becoming effective in competing against other people, not a belt colour which in kids classes really has little value yet the kids are misled to believe it makes them effective fighters.

text:
Nice to see the outward crescent kick being utilized. Hitting with the side of the instep is bone on bone after all, so just a light, flicking tap on the temple can certainly rock someone. Especially after consistent tempering on the makiwara, trees, etc.

Usually people neglect this technique, deeming it not to be that pragmatic, which is a shame, since it allows you to kick, and reach your opponent, from angles your feet otherwise wouldn't be able to reach. 

Plus, the more kicking-techniques you're prone to do, for example, the more confused your opponent will be, as to what direction you're kicking from. So it is a benefit to mix it up, and it makes you trickier.

Kyukushin Karate, along with some Okinawan styles of Karate in particular, are useful in the sense that, in the katas, they go deeper into the biomechanical principles of the techniques. This helps you unlock the full potential for power-generation.

This body-awareness, focus and zen-like state of mind, in conjunction with a comprehensive MMA training program is a very effective recipe, and may well turn out to be a hidden power in a modern environment where a lot of "old" training methods are neglected.

But not everyone can crack the traditional martial art's code, and thus be able to utilize its latent potential. Maybe people are too impatient and distracted nowadays, to develop that kind of gong fu...

text: I have never heard anybody say that traditional martial arts are useless. All martial arts stem from traditional martial arts. It is not a martial art that is slow, but the practitioner. The problem with mixed martial arts is that they are as the name implies, mixed. You can train in one martial art for decades and may never fully master it, though you would get good at it. If you try to train many at once the best you can hope for is to become a mediocre jack of all trades and master of none. As a handyman, a jack of all trades can fix many things, where as a master plumber can only fix plumbing, but can fix it better that than the jack of all trades. However in a fight to the death, mediocre dies at the hand of the master.  Training may be slow, because there are no shortcuts in getting good. Throwing a bunch of your favorite moves together and only learning those and calling it MMA does not prepare you for all situations. Most traditional martial arts have moves and techniques designed to handle a vast variety of situations however learning all of them in one particular art of style takes time and dedication. Doing 2 weeks of  training and paying exorbitant amounts of cash for a certificate that says you are a black belt as is widely practiced in the west, does not give you the skill, speed, stamina, precision, control and awareness that decades of repetitious training gives you. Doing ten pushups quickly lets you get them done in less time than doing them slowly, but doing them slowly builds more strength and stamina.

On average you learn your striking and grappling first, then your ground work and after that the scenarios begin where you're put in "real life" scenarios to prove your skills and gain experience. It's similar to sparring: Usually full contact with protection gear to simulate the stress and exhaustion of a real fight without injuring each other. You're also not put in weight classes, to make it more "realistic" by giving you different size and experience opponents. Apart from that the only difference to sparring is that you're sometimes in the corner of a room or start from the ground with someone above you OR have two guys attack you. Usually the goal is to get out of the situation fast and run away afterwards. Sometimes regular sparring is also implemented to focus on tequnique and fitness.

When Krav Maga was developed, it wasn't meant to be a style. It was a group of people training for survival, using whatever effective technique they could find. The training was pretty much MMA with street mindset: "we use what works, dump the rest". Therefore they sparred a lot, and were strong dedicated fighters. 

Then... They started to sell it outside Israel to civilians. Soccer moms and average joes don't really like to get hit for real, so the instructors started sparring less and less, afraid to lose students. It became an "theory based" technique because of that. The average students are too afraid to get hurt. Too much ego being sold the "ultimate self defense style" fallacy, and too little reality based tests. The only Krav Maga that is actually worth something today (with rare exceptions) is the military version, because soldiers are not afraid to train the hard way.

text: Mister Hanson, I served 12 years in Norway’s Jaegerkommandoen. One of the techniques we were taught as a component of our training among others was Krav Maga. This is a bit of info that I learnt decades ago during a training course I was taking: In the 1930s there was a young Ukrainian immigrant who was an electrical engineer and a physicist who also happened to be the first (or one of the first) Westerners to earn a black belt in Judo, and who actually started the first Western Judo Dojo in Paris France in the 1930s. His name was Moshe Feldenkrais (look him up, he's a very interesting character who was involved in all sorts of clandestine stuff during WWII). Anyway, forward a couple decades to after WWII and he's living in Israel now and is approached by 'powers that be' to help in devising a martial arts training program for the Army. 
In his observations over the years, he had noticed an interesting phenomenon that even his Judo experts all had a similar reaction when being attacked: the very first 'subconscious reflex' was to 'shy away' into a defensive stance from the attacker. He postulated that this was not only ineffective, but also a huge waste of energy, and spent a great deal of time figuring out how to change this up and 're-program' his students so that rather than 'shy away' they would instead react by 'moving straight in for the kill', so to speak, utilizing all of that powerful reflexive energy for attack purposes rather than for defensive purposes. Apparently it took quite a bit of re-orienting of training, muscle memory and reflexive habit to achieve this, but after a while the results began showing that by harnessing/reorienting the reflexive/defensive movement into an unconscious direct attack response, the results were dramatically improved. This all later evolved into advanced studies on "Neuro Plasticity in Modern Brain Research".  And this is what I was told was the very beginnings of the Krav Maga philosophy and style of fighting. 

I don't know for sure how accurate it is, but it was recounted to me by a retired combat veteran who had been an Israeli paratrooper back in the 60s; quite a formidable fellow, who was working now as a very highly regarded Feldenkrais-Method Trainer and Practitioner, and who seemed to be very credible. (Feldenkrais-Method is a sort of physical therapy/yoga/movement training discipline that is very popular overseas, especially in Australia and Europe, among physical therapists, trainers, and other rehab-type and movement-study (dancers, athletes, performers, chiropractors, etc) professionals. It's all very advanced; scientific, somatic, psychological, and just plain outright fascinating!)

I'd be interested in hearing anyone's thoughts or responses to all this, as I've never had a chance to research it in any way, aside from knowing that Mr Feldenkrais was indeed a very early western advocate and practitioner of Judo, and who also happened to be involved with all sorts of other historical people and events, including Madame Curie and also the early days of Manhattan Project! I don't know how much of this is common knowledge at this point, because I heard it all during private conversations 25+ years ago in NYC when I was studying the Feldenkrais-Method professional training/certification program myself.

I am 76. I began Karate at age 10 in Chicago in 1957. Shoryn Ryu. Got my first black belt at age 15. 
There was only white belt and black belt back then. No promotion fees. Went from 10th Kyu to 1rst Dan. 
Had to learn all the katas and weapons. No kids got a black belt till age 16. I was a rare exception.
Lots of light contact sparring. 
Started Japanese Jiu Jitsu at age 14. The Jiu Jitsu I learned was not a grappling sport. It was sort of a violent Aikido…. the object was to break bones and tear ligaments as you moved through your opponents. It fit perfectly with the karate I was studying. 

I later went into Shoto Kan and eventually settled into a no nonsense combat style called Sho Bo Kan.
By the time I joined the Navy at age 17 I could do 50 to 60 knuckle push ups on cement. 

I was in dozens of fights in grammar school and high school. My stuff worked. It was a time before the martial art# culture became popular. I was never a bully or a fight picker. I fought a lot of bullies. Took some good hits but I never lost. 

The trick to fighting is learning to stay in it. To concentrate in getting the job done in the maelstrom of violence. That’s why you see supposed martial arts masters get their ass kicked… they know techniques but they don’t know how to fight. Timing, distance, fakes, knowing how to extend but keep your balance… all essential fighting tools… and intent! You have to have the intent to injure, to disable. 

After a while it comes natural. My Vietnam combat experience added firearms to the personal arsenal. 

Last… any time you see a technic where the defender is working on one hand of the attacker while the attacker’s off hand is just hanging limp… realize that in a real fight that limp hand is going to be punching the side of your face or gauging your eye or stabbing your gut. 

In my late 20’s I fought bare knuckle about a dozen times. For money. Nothing but a crotch cup permitted. Later mouth guards were permitted… to protect a fighters hands from osteomyelitis after punching dirty teeth. I always won. Always got hurt. Fights were in a deserted factory building on west Ogden Ave. in Chicago. Made about 5 G’s per night. Quit when I had to shoot some guy in the parking lot after a fight night cause he insisted on being my manager.

I was in law school at the time. I didn’t need a manager. 

Got cut up by three guys at age 30 in a foreign county. Dispatched two handicapped one for life. I spent ten days in the hospital. Cost me a mint not to get charged. 

My last gun fight was in 2007 at age 60. Avoided a kidnapping in Juarez, Mexico. 

I have never picked a fight in my life and I am not a tac guy. I wear a suit and preppy clothes and I look like a mild mannered accountant. I have apologized to people getting in my face over a parking incident while being armed to the teeth. 

For some time I did some gov contracting but I found it too restrictive. Better money and less bosses in private work. Worked in a couple of “no prisoners taken” shitholes.

text: So, for some perspective: I was able to train some Krav Maga about 30 years ago by chance, very simplistic, and direct, guy had been in military, etc. I thought it had some good stuff. It is direct with little fluff. Like most martial arts, it hasn't really been tested en masse simply because most serious battle situations involved weaponry. But the Krav Maga being marketed to soccer moms here is mostly made up and unworkable beyond very basics. Basically to make it more complex, with belts, etc. they have included unworkable techniques. The ground stuff was almost non-existent back then and then of course, to make it workable, they stole from BJJ in the 1990s, etc. One would think if it was regularly battlefield and street tested it would have discovered that years ago. The one guys I know who can make any of it work are guys who train MMA, etc. And that is its problem; it really is only effective with other combative resistance arts like any other "traditional" art/method. But I think it is good for being quick and direct right off the bat. Some of its techniques, like knife defenses are truly garbage and terrible. Some have better ones (varies school to school). Also, it is interesting that quite a few of the older KM guys here claimed to be Israeli Special Forces, etc. and when investigated, their claims seem dubious at best. It's a whole industry now. Just train some boxing and grappling with a few strategies against weapons and that will serve you much better as an average person.

text:
Jason Hanson takes us back to the origins of Krav Maga and whys and hows of what is, "Essential Krav Maga".  Jason is advising against the road of complexity that some Krav Maga practitioners have followed, influenced by commercialization.
     Historic Krav Maga was intended to be the essence of simplicity and efficacy.  A person was confronted with an ambush-type of physical attack.  There was no time to engage in complex self-defense kata reactions; i.e. if this happens, then do this.  Original Krav Maga relied on the natural motor physical skills of the human body.
     As Jason reminded, historical Krav Maga was the bare bones fundamentals of essential physical self defense and protection encapsulated in week's or month's training at best, not ten to twenty years as advocated in Asian martial arts.
     As a matter of fact, in medieval Japan, the 14-year old son of a samurai warrior was now expected to perform fully functionally as a warrior.  Halfway across the world in feudal Normandy, the 14-year old son of a Norman knight was now expected to be a ready man-at-arms as his father.  Does this sound like ten to twenty years of intensive training, meditation, apprenticing in Shaolin temples, or anything else like that?  One learned the skills to survive quickly or you didn't survive.
     Sounds familiar?  Anyone remember Defendu?  Remember its founder, Assistant Police Commissioner of Shanghai, William E. Fairbairn, circa 1921.  At that time Shanghai was one of the world's most dangerous cities to live, if not the most dangerous city where human life was cheap and anything was for sale.  Having survived numerous physical attacks as a policeman in dangerous Shanghai leaving his body and hands crisscrossed with innumerable scars, Fairbairn distilled his core Jujutsu training with western boxing, wrestling, and French Savate.  He named his eclectic self-defense regimen, "Defendu".  It was not a martial art just as Krav Maga is really not a martial art.  It is a self-protection/self-defense physical regimen.
    Both Defendu and Krav Maga were taught in a matter of weeks.  All were strictly counter-offensive self-defense.  It presumed the attacker got to you first.  There are no blocks in the systems.  The basis is immediate, harsh counter-offense.  End the fight in seconds.  This is not a MMA match.  The goal is to survive and end the fight as fast as possible.
     In today's Krav Maga studios you see students kitted out with head pads, gloves, knee pads, etc.  In original Krav Maga, taught to the civilian militia members of the early Israeli State and its immediate predecessors, people simply learned by practicing with each other on mats or grass, soft earth, or sand in outdoors training areas, wearing their civilian clothing or rudimentary military uniforms.  Training did not take years.  It did not take a year.  We're talking more like weeks.  It might have been months for some of those people but no more.  There was no time to become a deadly master after ten years of training.
    Historic Defendu was the same.  Fairbairn created Defendu to be taught in weeks' time of intensive instruction and practice.  He later revised Defendu for wartime usage, meaning it was more deadly.  It was taught to British commandos, American and Canadian rangers, special forces, Navy divers, and the OSS.  Many of today's military hand-to-hand combatives can trace their origins far back to Defendu, even indirectly through past combat instructors who passed their knowledge down through generations of younger military combat instructors who learned other skills and added those to create new modern military combatives.  But if you research even the modern ones today carefully, you'll likely find some trace back to Defendu.  Much of that is because the core art of Defendu was Japanese Jujutsu, which itself is a distant core art to many if not most modern military hand-to-hand combatives.

Additionally, 75% of Krav Maga is just Muay Thai, BJJ, Wrestling, some Judo and only 25% are modified Japanese JuJutsu or original Krav Maga techniques. It was created to get someone (a new soldier) with zero combat training to basic fighting compacity within a short period of time. It's not made to make you into a MMA fighter. Most Krav Maga practitioners generally use Krav Maga as a introduction to martial arts and after about a year, move on to combat sports. They will go back to Krav Maga for self-defense and scenario based training (I followed the same path and currently use it for that reason too).

text:
I train Krav Maga and at my Dojo they put emphasis on the following prerequesites to learn KM:
- The curriculum is greenlighted by the International Krav Maga Foundation. We have direct ties with Israels best instructors and practitioners. The men that train us here had to get their testing done in Israel itself before they were even allowed to teach and call themselves experts. All of our instructors are also black belts in many a different martial arts so they have experience beyond just KM. The lads that train me for instannce are black belts in: jiujitsu, judo, pencan silat or taekwondo. (So they know self defence from more than just one angle so I believe their arguments and my own experience when stating that Krav Maga can be useful.)
- Make your attacks realistic: if you punch for training simulations: try to hit your target and use recoil. (Ofcourse you start slowing and build up with beginners) No one learns to deflect strikes if they miss in the first place because you are aiming at thin air. Chokes, mounts, headlocks, bearhugs or any raw type of physical agression must be done with 'force'. If you are not really strangling someone and your target can escape by just stepping backwards, you are not teaching them anything. (Naturally you make sure you are not permanently damaging someone.) Stuff like this really reminds you how difficult it can be to escape let's say a rear naked choke and how little time you have. But it adds allot to learning how to fight if you ask me. 
- We have scenario training: in bars, on the streets or simulating loud clubs in sports halls (big crowd, loud music, disco lights). We do multiple attackers vs 1 combat drills, defending a VIP that is under attack (your buddy that doesn't do anything) and sparring to learn how to deal with pressure etc. We deliberately add stuff like being verbally agressive towards someone as well. Not just start pushing someone, scream at them and insult them at the same time. Other examples include that while you are sparring with someone 1 vs 1 another person can come in from behind to start and choke you. Or while you are trying to release yourself you can still be attacked with punches/kicks from other kravists. They put allot of emphasis on scanning your environment: how many people are there, don't get isolated or cornered and always look for an exit. 
- Krav Maga focuses on easy to employ movements because under stress you small motor skills go straight out of the window. Most techniques are simultaneous attacks and defences and can be performed under 2 seconds. So no elaborate 20 steps nonsense to 'end a fight quickly'. I have a background in judo and jiujitsu and I am convinced the Krav techniques are cleaner, faster and more painful than any of the self defences I was taught in those other schools of fighting. (Not saying that judo and jiujitsu are bad)

I also like to add that Krav doesn't reinvent the wheel. There are kicks, punches, armbars, chokes, releases and throws that come straight from boxing, muay thai, wrestling and jiujitsu. For instance the before mentioned curriculum has techniques like roundhouse kicks, side/back/low kicks, uppercuts, jabs, hooks, knee strikes and many more that are used in other martial arts. What it does add though is a pinch of realism that you can expect on the streets: people wearing shoes, people having hidden weapons, multiple opponents and not obeying any strict rules. So in Krav we target weakspots on the body where other defence systems won't allow it. Think about the groin, eyes, throat etc so you will have your own tools to fight back. So during sparring you are allowed to kick someone in the nuts however most of it looks arguably very similar to MMA. I like to think that krav maga teaches you allot about fighting and gives you many tools to defend yourself. What makes it unique is that it doesn't shy away from using dirty fighting and does allot with you alone vs many. (It's scary how heavy it is to fight 1 vs 5 for just 2 minutes, you will be out of breath) Even Bas Rutten himself said that he would defend himself in a barfight by starting out with a headbutt: no fancy stuff just let them know you are not messing around. Sports fighting is not the same as street fighting. Krav leans towards the latter that's why there are no medals to win in tournaments. 

The downside is I have constantly blue spots and scratches all over my body. I am thankful for the protection we wear like tonques, mouth guards, shin guards and sometimes MMA or boxing gloves. But I think it proves that we try to make our defensive tactcs realistic. Hope that adds my two cents. Thanks allot for the video mate! As a final note I would like to add that all the things you mentioned in your thesis apply to any martial art in general. You can find plenty of videos on YouTube about instructions and techniques from other disciplines were during the demonstration the opponent offers little to no resistance and people just standing there waiting to be 'taken down'. Does this mean jiujitsu is shit now as well? You can easily manipulate footage to make a fool out of any martial art or make anyone looks like a total beginner if you just focus on the bad parts. Just search for any judo/sambo video where they teach you a throw. No one is offering resistance there because they are for showing the technique for starters. Doesn't mean judo doesn't work as a sport in a 1 vs 1 duel where both are struggling each other. Doesn't mean you can take someone out on the street by throwing them over your shoulder on the pavement. How is this for proof that Krav Maga works as a system: in my country they teach it to police officers, security guards and soldiers too. Hell, some of my instructors are directly hired by local law inforcement to teach some krav maga. Those professionals share plenty of examples of encounters at the job where they succesfully employed krav maga to keep themselves safe. So can that prove the system has it's uses? Or do a few internet videos make the whole thing a scam?

text:
This pretty much boils down, from my experience, to whether we're talking about "real" Israeli Krav Maga or about the watered down version, seen in many places around the world.

Krav Maga is a tried, true  and well tested method developed for the IDF and is the only martial art taught here. During training, we pressure test everything, we run complex, real scenario drills, simulations and fighting with everything we learn and it is tested by fire every single day on the streets by military and law enforcement across the country. This mentality is preserved in most civilian Krav Maga places around Israel.

Jake from Armchair Violence has what I think is a really good central point about this: Krav Maga is not a fighting system with a syllabus of techniques, it's a philosophy with a set of principles. That makes choosing to train in Krav unreliable even compared to arts like aikido because there's no consistency.

To illustrate my point, if you go to a boxing class you can be fairly certain you'll be taught a jab, cross and hook, and you'll likely be taught them under at least the pressure of sparring. If you go to a BJJ class you'll be taught the guard and an armbar, and you'll learn to apply them in rolling. If you go to aikido you'll be taught kote gaeshi and tegatana, and you'll probably only learn to apply them in low-pressure randori. On the other hand, if you go to a Krav class, you might be taught any, all or none of those, under a wildly varying amount of pressure and anywhere from no protective gear to full armour, depending on the background of the instructor, because *calling it Krav Maga only means you're teaching according to Krav principles*.

To be clear, this isn't to say that there aren't good and bad instructors and places from which to learn other martial arts, but the problem is endemic to Krav because it explicitly has no standard curriculum or training methods.

At least in my federation, FEKM, and the video misses some important points:
-the knife defense technique (indeed all the weapon techniques) includes a simultaneous strike/series of strikes (including groin) intended to stun and therefore allow some time for escape or joint manipulation. Of course doing a wrist lock is not going to be very effective cold, but in the wake of a boot point to the testicles...
-sparring is routine, mandatory and includes hard sparring for the level tests;
-the sparring includes standard MMA style but also groin strikes and on the ground we lose the gloves and go for eyes, groin etc. and includes all illegal moves from MMA (you fight like you train, right?)
-Obviously techniques "working" is not a binary... "working" in Krav means that the initial attack was mitigated and you have inflicted pain or damage in return and you are in a better position (posture, body position, etc) afterwards than before
-we absolutely pressure test/scénario train on a regular basis (blind siding, multiple attackers, backed into corner, multiple attacks in series, use of objects and obstacles, etc.)

Finally, Krav Maga is a series of principles more than techniques: Develop aggressive attitude once the first attack happens; simultaneous defense and strike to invert the dynamic of the altercation asap; prioritize "dirty" attacks to eyes, throat, groin, knee, etc. Prioritize shortest path of motion; Objective is always neutralize to escape (not look pretty, get involved in some sort of stupid dominance display, etc.).

Krav/self defense gyms also attract many people with NO martial arts or sport experience (often women/bullied teens/nerdy guys) who are looking to develop confidence. Going from a reaction of "shell up, give up your back and hope it ends soon" to "stay out of strike range, get your hands up, block a haymaker/react to a choke, inflict some degree of damage then GTFO or square up in a proper fighting stance with basic foot work and jab/cross/front kicks and go for the throat eyes and groin if you can" is a HUGE step forward for the majority of beginning Krav students.

text:
Krav Maga schools that teach realistic self defense spar.  It is that simple.

By sparring, I don't mean hitting pads!!?!  I mean trading unscripted light punches with an actively resisting live training partner, keeping the power of the striking low enough that you don't injure each other.  I think, up to levels of tolerable discomfort, is probably the sweet spot to learn how to hit without being hit, without injuring your training partner.

Without this vital learning experience of how to hit without being hit, you wouldn't be able to spot an opening and gain an advantage over an attacker whose fists are flying at you like a windmill.

Why has Krav Maga attracted so many negative comments about its functionality?  As a Krav Maga practitioner, I would like to explain.  THERE IS AN UNREASONABLY LONG INDUCTION PERIOD BEFORE ALLOWING STUDENTS TO SPAR!  I started training in Krav at a school under the IKMF syllabus, and IIRC the IKMF demand that students grade TWICE(!) before even being allowed to slow spar.  In fact, I'm not sure if they're even allowed to do basic sparring drills like practising very light jab/cross, the other person slipping and evading, and then swapping round.  Even that would give at least some basic introduction to hitting without being hit.  But I don't think they're even allowed to do that until they've passed the P1 and P2 tests.  It would take a person with an average level of attendance at least a year and a half to reach this stage.  I would imagine the average person has a finite window of their life to give to self defense training.  Might I suggest 1 to 2 years, averagely, guess what, a year and a half?  Consequently, MOST KRAV MAGA STUDENTS NEVER SPAR!  Consequently, most Krav students don't have the first clue how to slip and evade a beating, let alone how to counterpunch a moving target that's trying to evade them.

And it is this mismanagement of protocol, that causes keyboard warriors to frequently ask questions like, "Is Krav Maga legit?", "Is Krav Maga a joke?", "Is Krav Maga BS?".

Believe it or not, the school I was in before didn't spar at all, anyway, no matter how high you graded.  Now, I'm joining a school that trains under the Krav Maga Global syllabus.  That allows you to, at least, slow spar after grading only once and attending, I think, 30 lessons.  Now, that's clearly better than the IKMF, but it's still too long in my opinion.  I think, any Krav instructor worth his or her salt, ought to be able to look at a student, and determine within about 3 months of reasonably consistent attendance whether that student has good control, is not reckless or malicious, and can therefore be trusted in a sparring class.  I think to string it out any longer than that serves no purpose.

Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face.  And no amount of pre-scripted drills against a willing, compliant, static partner will do anything to change that.  Not allowing students access to sparring of any kind in a timely and fair fashion is what is causing Krav to be called into question all the time.

I've trained my fair share of Krav Maga. Real KM is not beautiful, technical, masterful and precise. It's violent, dirty, ugly, sloppy and chaotic.

- You'll always get cut in a knife fight and your chances of survival are slim
- Disarming an opponent ONLY works if the opponent is not set to kill you, otherwise you're dead already (robbery, assault, etc.)
- Gun disarm is a russian roulette. You go for it and hope for the best.

I've dipped my feet a little bit in Krav maga and there were some issues from my own experience. It should first teach you combat principles, similar to what you learn in combat sports as a whole (especially live sparring and conditioning). If you're put in a situation where you need to physically defend yourself (no other option), you need to know how to fight. You need proper combat techniques, conditioning, strategy, etc (essentially combat sports training). But the thing that should separate Krav from combat sports training is the situation training. You hit the nail on the head here. 

It's really the situation training, like getting jumped from the back, assessing threats, etc. that should be focused after combat principles have been established. I come from a muay Thai and boxing background (and a little bit of grappling) and my training in these arts will give me advantages in defense situations IF I'm squared up and ready to go. However getting jumped from out of nowhere, attacked by multiple people. Or situations where weapons are involved are not things addressed in combat sports (and we all know this). Youre focused on beating one person. My conditioning and training will help but sometimes it might not be enough. This is where KM has to thrive and focus on. It's a shame because Krav maga on paper sounds good, but the way schools teach it is the complete opposite. 

The strong focus on these knife/gun disarm techniques and lack of pressure testing/sparring is really where it falls short. It's better than nothing (if I'm being optimistic) but those disarm techniques need to be constantly pressure tested so that schools can really hone in on how to properly teach them and dispose the garbage techniques. That and live sparring would go a LLLLOONNNGGG way in improving KM. Once that's done they should focus on situational training like how the SPEAR system does. Just my two cents.

From a business standpoint, I don't think KM should ever be it's own school. It should part of a general martial arts gym. Imagine a gym where you have boxing classes, kickboxing classes, grappling classes and even weapons based classes like fencing, HEMA, arnis, etc. Then on a different day you have self defense/ Krav maga classes where you take all that you learned from the previous classes and train it in different situations where instead of focusing on in-ring situations, you focus on scenarios that would happen on the street. One can only dream of such a gym.

text: This is so true. I spent 17 years working as an officer for a UK government body, during which time I spent approximately 8 years on riot response and around 7 or 8 years as a use of force instructor. As such my specialism was control and restraint, as was virtually everyone elses, with one on one personal protection playing a part in that syllabus. I can confirm that genuine duress and pressure testing is the only real measure of a systems effectiveness and the only way to condition your natural responses is to make a system usable under stress. But you'd be surprised how little training it took to get people to be able to deal with most, "Martial artists." But highly trained Martial artists, street fighters, well practiced MMA fighters and boxers, were way more difficult to deal with. In short, people who actually fought as part of their training. And don’t even get me started on weapons, it was my favourite subject to teach and to study, but I can confirm that the first time someone pulls an edged weapon on you for real your brain turns to porridge and gross motor skills are about the best you can manage without being way more highly specialised and crucially, pressure tested than I was. Don't get me wrong, we still dealt with it, but my god does it open your eyes to exactly how much bullshit is taught around this subject. If you want an interesting eye opener, and you haven't already done it, try and get some training in with people who have to deal with these threats in real life on a regular basis.
