With it's modern name recognition, Krav often feels like Karate's edgier brother.  And just as with Karate, there are a lot of bad schools out there and you really need to shop the teacher, not just the style.  I'm fortunate that I ended up at a good one and it initially surprised me to learn the reputation Krav has now. I actually joined the gym mostly for Krav at first but the stuff we were doing was so tough for me that I decided to just focus on Muay Thai (where our head coaches have been pro fighters) for about a year to get my conditioning up before returning to Krav classes.  One of our current Krav teachers has a Dutch kickboxing background and the other is also a Muay Thai coach at the gym. Most of the class time is devoted to basic strikes or occasionally basic BJJ or wrestling.  I'd say a third is then used for self-defense scenarios such as being choked, grabbed, or otherwise attacked by surprise.  We used to have a basic and more advanced class for Krav, but the pandemic has kind of squished all the students together.  Both the coaches highly recommend students do the Muay Thai and BJJ classes offered but the reality is that many students don't have the time or funds to do that so we have to spend most of the class time doing what is basically crude MMA but with the option to kick the groin or guard pass by punching the groin. My 2 cents: Krav Maga is not a martial art, it is a type of close combat. It is about attacking as defence (or attacking as attack). If not done aggressively to hurt the other, it is just not effective. It's about survival and not defence; about "sometimes risking breaking your arm, but stop a crowbar hitting your face". The fear in a real fight enhances it. That can only be well trained in (almost) military environments.

Also, in a sport-situation you are not allowed do use like 60% of the techniques; as eye, airpipe, ears and all other sensitive areas are not allowed to be targeted. Same thing as the Spetsnaz Systema, as a "sport" or "martial art" it is just funny, but if you are in a dark street in a war zone, the physical training, basic techniques and conditioned attitude do the job. KM is about running to the fight when needed (because you must and your officers have an objective to meet) and not about points or least-damage. 

End of the day, whatever the style,  it is always about stamina, speed, some experience, grappling, kicking and boxing. 

May (if your case is right) your brothers & sisters have your back and be with more as the other guys.

Mind conditioning is, or at least was, the major selling point of KM.  When KM began being popular, what made it different was the idea that w/o mind conditioning, all body conditioning and technique learning is useless in self defence, unless, it's a situation in which you are given the time to prepare for a fight.    Even very good fighters need some time to reset their mind to 'fighting mode', as you clearly pointed out in your video. In an emotions driven situation (basicly when you're not a fighting mindset and you are caught by surprise) even MMA fighters revert to some instict-driven brawl like they forgot all their training.

It takes time to those people to switch to technical fighting mode, and that's even more true for those disciplines that are less fight oriented (by that I mean, you can have a sport "fight", but the more rules you have to remember, the more different your mindset it from real world brawls).

I clearly remember that training real world scenarios, including simulating stress conditions, was a strong part of the original KM philosophy.  Not only real full resistance practicing (like randori in Judo), but even simulating certain conditions, like doing that after you overexercize yourself, starting while being already out of breath. Back in the the days, I heard they even used alchool to induce confusion and slow reflexes.

It goes w/o saying that while useful, this type of practicing is also on average way more dangerous.  Part of the reason Judo and BBJ get away with lots of "rolling" is that it happens in full control, in a relatively relaxed context.  The same activity under real stress conditions has inherently a much higher injury ratio.

That's probably why many school dropped that part of the training.

I would say even BJJ had a similar evolution. I was there when the BJJ craze started. One of BJJ selling points (compared to Judo) was that no techniques were banned. Over the years, as it became popular and widespread, they started banning dangerous stuff too.

I've been a Thai boxer all my adult life (I'm 57 now). I hold a brown belt in judo and a blue belt in BJJ. I've practiced Krav Maga (I lived in Israel for 2 years). And what I've found is that all instructors were themselves accomplished martial artists before they started Krav Maga. Anyone who was somewhat adept in another art would do okay in Krav Maga. But people who have never done any martial art will mostly suck as a fighter practicing just Krav Maga. Unless the instructor teaches the basics from (kick)boxing and grappling, you will not become a good fighter.
For basic self defense, it's better than nothing. If the instructor exposes you to stress testing, like they do in the army, you will at least stay cool under pressure, which is very valuable. Krav Maga is not intended to teach you to fight another accomplished fighter. But there simply is no replacement for sparring and other forms of stress testing.

Conflict of interest: Krav Maga instructor in Europe.
Krav Maga is a self-defense system. Let's talk about Krav Maga for civilians, as far as I know about it in my organisation.
Krav Maga has certain principles which need to be met in every technique in order for it to be the most effective. Following the classes the practitioners become familiar which the principles. The Krav Maga principles can certainly be taught in a short amount of time, because they are simple. But one cannot think they know and understand them fully in a short amount of time.
This discussion does not revolve around a main pillar of Krav Maga: self-defense in reality based attacks. In big organisations these defenses (but not only these) form the curriculum which helps civilians address the most common problems in the streets. Before fighting you must escape the initial problem, attack or threat effectively. We emphasize on that, because it's a matter of life and death, for example if someone chokes you or tries to lift you up and take you to the ground.
Other aspects are fighting, tactical fighting, tactics, and fitness.
Do you need sparring? Yes. Do you need to know when you should be aggressive? Yes. Do you need to know how to deal multiple attackers? Yes. Do you need to improve physically? Yes.
Problem 1: Certificates. In sports you can find an instructor who has competed and/or has trained good athletes. What about Krav Maga?
I choose to be a student in my current organisation because it met the following criteria:
They had a rich curriculum, they had a realistic approach, they had good short simple answers to big problems, they had a super method of teaching, thus making me progress fast, they were not afraid to say "these techniques are very difficult", they were doing updates and making their techniques better, the instructors were trained directly under the main instructors of Imi (the founder of Krav Maga in Israel), the instructors were tested themselves and evolved as students, they did sparring,  and many more... In my eyes that was a legit self-defense system.
What is "good" Krav Maga? Krav Maga which follows the aforementioned principles.
What's a good Krav Maga instructor? Someone who wants to know, who wants to be tested under pressure, who keeps being trained. Does he need to know other systems?
In my opinion he must know about all legit systems/sports, and to train himself in striking and grappling so that he can be a good all around fighter.

I've been reviewing a lot of combat material and had the opportunity to practice Karate, Capoeira and Boxing when i was younger (I'm 32 now).
After being presented to Krav Maga by a co-worker, started working on it and did it consecutive for 5 years. I went to what was called to be the official center (Federação Sulamericana de Krav Maga - I'm brazillian BTW) and got extremely lucky to have one of the best, if not the best teacher that that federation had. 
The concept was that we were going to learn the practical fundamentals on almost every other martial art (boxing, karate kicks, aikido forms, police grappling and so forth) so you would be a well-rounded guy.
The progress was not fast as everyone advertises (and I'm pretty certain part of it was for monetization purposes, but i understand the responsibility to put someone on the street and say that you have the tools for self defending against whatever) but my instructor wouldn't take easy on anyone. He and the class was indeed fit and trained as a proper athlete training should be IMO. He would only put you to the exam if you've actually mastered the content and regularly tested you against the others in sparring sessions. And that discrepancy of level of instructors was extremely evident during the exams. Some students (even advanced in grade) wouldn't even put some push-ups together with a proper form...
I understand now that Krav Maga has a huge deficiency on ground fight as per the philosophy that was taught me which prays that in the crowd or in a environment you do not control, going down exposes you a lot (and indeed it does) but its important for one on one situations where you have control of your surroundings to have a decent amount of ground work, which is why I'm working on my jiu-jitsu nowadays.

text:
Nice interview!
FWIW, I taught BJJ  & grappling at the national headquarters for two separate  Krav Maga Organizations. (About 7 years between the two schools).  I have taught many KM students & instructors. I have taught at KM instructor training camps and, even today, a couple of my students are Wingate Institute certified KM Black Belt instructors. IMO, the techniques of Krav Maga are OK - not amazing-- but fine. The main problems I've seen with KM people are: 1) An inability to function in chaos. Everything tends to be  presented as a specific response to a specific attack --it's very technique heavy. 2) Overconfidence. A Lot of KM people are naive about real fighting. They think a violent attack is easy to solve with a nice technique, because they haven't gotten a lot of realistic feedback.


Also, FWIW, KM tends to attract a different "type" of students than a typical BJJ, Judo, MMA or kickboxing gym.People who are "afraid" of training somewhere like an MMA gym, yet also want to be Jason Bourne. There is a lot of "fantasy" in the training. I was teaching a room full of Km School owners and one guy clearly faked an injury to get out of grappling. I mentioned it to the head of the Assn and he said, "He always has an injury when it's time to grapple".  Later that day I saw him practicing LITERALLY the rear Machine gun takeaway where you LIFT YOUR OPPONENT in the air and slam him on his face to disarm him. To me, that;s a LOT of KM people. I think the narrative that there is "tha REAL" Krav Maga out there that is bad-ass & functional is very much like the narrative that there is "tha REAL" Wing Chun out there that is bad-ass & functional.


KM also does a lot of drills that FEEL like hard sparring, but aren't. It's always set up so that you "win". Unlike in BJJ, Judo, Wrestling, kickboxing, MMA, etc you don't ever get "humbled" in a KM school. You don't get that EXTREMELY important experience of trying your very best and failing. You always prevail because your partner, the coach etc will lower standard of the drill until you "succeed". that is VERY different than sparing


Also, while both of the schools I taught at offered BJJ & kickboxing, the kickboxing both places was taught by KM instructors who came up in the same kickboxing class they were teaching. People who had ZERO fighting experience in the ring, in competition or anywhere, teaching others.  KM as taught IS a "martial art" in every way. The dynamics are identical to that of any TMA school I have trained at. And, again, this was at the HQ of two of the bigger KM orgs.

text: I have attended 3 to 6 classes a week for a year (until the Coronavirus came along, that is) at BR Krav Maga in Baton Rouge, Louisiana.  It is one of the REAL Krav Maga schools in the nation that teach REAL Krav Maga & not just something someone threw together & called it Krav Maga to make a buck off the latest trend.  The instructors at BR Krav Maga are real people, not taking on any arrogance & not putting on a show just to impress the new people.  They are each very well trained in the particular class that they are trusted with teaching, whether it's Krav Maga Fundamentals, Sparology (boxing), Fitness (kickboxing), From the Ground Up (wrestling & BJJ) or one of the many weapons classes on Fridays.  Besides the realism of the instructors & the training, I enjoy the fact that everyone gets the chance to learn all of the material that is available at the school -- whether you're a beginner or a black belt.  The promotions & ranking depends on what level of the material you are currently working on.  If you're lookin' for a REAL Krav Maga school, ask Ryan or any of the other trainers at Fit To Fight to point you in the right direction.  That's where my instructors go to learn new things so that they can improve on their awesomeness.  I trained in karate years ago & this is totally different.  In REAL Krav Maga, there's no uniforms, no formations with black belts in front & white belts in the back, & there's no insistence on bowing to the mat or anyone there.  The instructors are just as concerned about earning your trust as you are about earning theirs.  I wouldn't train anywhere else!   One other thing that I enjoy about Krav Maga is that we're not training for any competitions with rules, we're training for REAL street fighting.

text: I suppose that I am fortunate to practice KM at a really, really good center then (in Sweden). I'd like to add a few things that I really appreciate with KM, at least from my club, and that is that we practice the "psychology of violence". We practice how to avoid violence; de-escalation. Many of us attending the training are average Joes/Joettes who have never been in a fight, as such we find it hard to deliver the first strike, but when de-escalation doesn't work you need to be prepared to deliver the first blow. That is darn hard to come to grips with, but we practice that. We get exposed to "100% violence" (with helmets, mouth guard and gloves) from one or more aggressors and we are conditioned to never effing give up. On top of this we of course have the actual techniques, which are kept simple and to a low number so that we actually might use them in a panicked situation. But "failing a technique" is also part of the training scheme, or rather, problem solving; if we fail to perform a specific technique we are never allowed to go "Oh, shoot, I messed it up. Let's take it from the start". When that happens you have a training buddy and/or instructor yelling "Solve the effing problem!!". And yes, you instructors are police, security guards etc. who have experienced a fair share of violence.

text: I did Krav Maga for a couple of years, and I really enjoyed it. I came to it having done Mok Gar kung fu as a teen, then jiujitsu at university. I can't really comment on the state of KM in the USA but there are a few federations or associations that have a "lineage" directly from Imi Lichtenfeld. As others have said, Imi put the system together when he was a young man in Bratislava, trying to protect  the Jewish community from attack by Nazi thugs. His dad was the local police chief, and he'd learned boxing & wrestling, but he found when people are coming after you with clubs & knives your basic boxing isn't quite up to the job. Krav Maga has been constantly evolving ever since, but its core techniques are boxing, wrestling, jiujitsu & muay thai. The main organisations you should look for are those headed by the people Imi taught directly. They have a core syllabus that teaches the techniques Imi came up with. They usually maintain a close association with the IDF, too - you'll see them teaching KM to the IDF, and getting feedback on the success or otherwise of the techniques when IDF soldiers use it in the field. The club I used to go to, which my kids go to now, started out as an IKMF club, but I believe is now part of Krav Maga Worldwide. Both are reputable organisations. My own teacher's pre-KM background was jiujitsu and Sambo (the Russian grappling system) so their ground game is pretty good. They spar with gloves and gumshields. Many of their instructors cross-train in sport martial arts, and they encourage folks to go do muay thai, go do jiujitsu, widen their horizons.

Krav is mainly meant to get yourself out of a dangerous situation, either by de-escalating the situation or by countering an attack and then getting the hell out of there after throwing at most three punches and a kick to create an opening to run. If you put practitioners of both in a room and tell them to fight, then probably the person who's always training for just such a situation is going to come out on top.

Man, I get so worn out with these pointless arguments about which discipline is the 'best'. When you do this, u do a disservice to the many good martial arts that do exist. As for km itself, you probably won't find many mma fighters that train solely in this background because it's not designed for the ring. It's designed for the military, law enforcement, violent street self-defense and so forth. I've done bjj and judo, and currently km for the past two years, and all 3 are excellent martial arts, but very different in their styles. Km isn't some discipline that is better than everything else. It's simply a fighting system that draws upon various techniques of many martial arts. It's a system that says, hey, some of that bjj groundwork is excellent, some of those judo throws work great, man those kicks from taekwondo or muay thai are really effective, so let's incorporate those. And along the way, we'll introduce how to defend against knife, gun, and stick weapon threats, how to effectively break an attacker's neck, his wrist or arm, how to attack the eyes, throat and groin, how to learn situational awareness, etc. All things that would never be allowed in a sanctioned sport. It's not that km is 'better' than everything else, it's just that it make more sense for the desired objectives. Pretty much all legitimate martial arts require years of training to become truly proficient, so km said, let's draw upon many of these other arts and find techniques that limit the use of fine motor skills that are lost during an adrenaline dump and instead focus on those that utilize more gross motor movements. Let's also find techniques that tend to more closely mimic the instinctive reactions of people. Skills we can teach in a much quicker time frame. So when someone asks me every once in awhile if I could defeat an mma fighter, my response is, god, I sure wouldn't think so. That individual is a trained fighter. It's what he or she lives for, so why would I think my km could just mop up this other person with ease? Those of us in the martial arts world need to stop these arguments about who has the best system and instead recognize the contributions each disciple brings to us all.

text: Joe Rogans words stem from ignorance. I don’t think ge is talking smack, or has any I’ll intention here, but he just doesent know what Krav is really about, nor has he practiced with a real Krav practitioner or Instructor. Krav was formed using Ju-Jitsu, Judo, Aikido, Muy Thai, and boxing. The better training facilities also offer Kali/Silat classes, Brazilian Ju-Jitsu classes, and more to its students. I don’t know where Joe Rogan got his information but he truly has no idea what Krav is all about. It’s not about “biting someone” Krav is meant for extreme cases of Self-Defense. Krav is taught with the main intention of disabling your opponent and ending the fight as quickly as possible. Krav teaches its practitioners how to Kill their opponent. Sure he might punch me, or try and choke me out… but Krav has taught me to react quickly, simultaneously, parry, counter the incoming punch while I am grabbing his throat and with all my power squeezing and ripping out his Adam’s apple… or when he’s trying to choke me, I’m takeing my fingers and gouging the eyeballs out of his head. If he is successful in taking me down, then it’s a good thing Krav teaches all of the most essential and effective parts of Judo, Aikido, and his beloved Brazilian Ju-Jitsu. They don’t just teach the techniques, they also teach the mentality to fight, and to kill. They teach you the intensity, and then practice it full on 100% because the only way to Be able to perform in a real situation, is to have been in that situation before and know what it’s like. You have to know what it feels like to have someone choke you out with all their might. Krav was formed and taught so that people would survive. There’s a reason why Navy Seals were/are taught Krav. I grew up with one of the scariest, most intense, strongest, and most intelligent human beings on earth( he’s the real life Superman) and he was the captain of a seal team. The seals he was with were a different breed even from the seals today, who are all over social media bragging and being all cool to make money. Guess what he was taught… you guessed right.. Krav. Sure if you go to Steven Segal to learn krav it’s probably going to look funny and look like a joke. But it’s a whole different story when you go to an instructor who is is one of the deadliest people on earth. It’s different when you are instructed in a country that’s surrounded by people that say “death to the Jews” every single day when they wake up and go to sleep, who have rockets launches into their country every day, who sneak weapons in, or even take knives and try to kill as many Jewish men, women, and kids as they can, who are not only fighting for their families, they are fighting to make sure that their country, their culture, their way of life is not completely wiped out from existance.. these people are fighting to make sure that another holocaust absolutely will not happen again… and everyday they are willing to die defending their people…. When you go take Krav-Maga in a place like that, and your being trained by soldiers who are defending their mothers and fathers, spouses and children every day… then it’s a whole different story. It’s alot more then just “biting”  and not a martial art to be taken lightly. There’s a reason it’s been trained to the most elite soldiers in the world, and still is to this day.  I think Joe is right about a lot of things, but this is something he is completely wrong about, and he should do a little bit more research before speaking on it again. I would advise that instead of going to the Hollywood Krav Maga center for Celebrities… or the SuperKrav center for schmucks… that he take a trip to Israel, and set up a special training deal for a few weeks, and then come back and see what he thinks of it.

text:
I would go for Dutch style kickboxing rather than muy thai MT is a beautiful art with powerful kicks and strikes and heavy clinch work and ellbows, but it’s built around engaging in exchanges. You *communicate* with your opponent you kick, they kick, you block, they counter. It’s rhythmic and power-based, and you're grounded in close range.

Dutch kickboxing took the foundations of MT (especially the low kicks and ellbows and clinch) but evolved it into a faster, more mobile, in-and-out system. Dutch fighters are lighter on their feet, throw quick boxing combinations ending in low kicks, and rely less on standing and trading. It’s more pressure based and fluid, less about waiting for a return exchange.

Historically, the dutch actually trained in mt in the 70s then blended it with western boxing (which is always good) and kyokushin karate that’s why their footwork, angles, and combo flow are so different.

So yeah, MT might hit harder, but dutch-style kickboxing moves smarter.

So I rather go with that. I train it myself for years and I really like being mobile wouldnt trade it. Still I respect the power of muy thai trust me I do.

text:
What I always like to say is the best martial art is whichever one you can train, whatever is near you whatever you enjoy enough to stick around etc. And I agree that boxing has the best/most skilled hands of the popular martial arts and the arts I know, and I would agree that from what I’ve seen and done taekwondo has the most variety of kicks and the most skill in them, but I think Muay Thai gives you very solid skills in both worlds plus elbows knees and sweeps if where you train does clinch (which it should) so personally if you could only train one I’d recommend and train Muay Thai. I would like to add though that taekwondo now is more for the sport than not but I do wanna say that by no means do I think taekwondo and karate don’t work but I also do know that they are more sport focused than true battle in its roots (not granted all arts nowadays that are popular are primarily for sport but still) as that’s just the way it went in Japan at that time, still perfectly effective but just a note. (And that’s kinda the difference between jutsu and do which if I recall was like in the beginning of the edo period in Japan when they finally had peace they tried to restrict what combat training people could do with weapons and unarmed and all that so it became more sport focused but my memory isn’t the best and that’s just a side note ramble because I found it interesting when my kenjutsu (katana art the style I train is from 1336 I believe) sensei taught me that). But that being said most martial arts at least in the US train focusing on a 1v1 in a ring and say how you’d adapt it for self defense and hardly ever take into account deliberately training for fighting people of other styles of fighting and multiple opponents etc, but correct me if I’m wrong. Rambling aside I think for striking if you can only do one Muay Thai and striking is more important for say MMA or street defense at least in a situation where you have space but grappling is very important especially for self defense like if someone sneaks up and grabs you and for that my personal preference is jujutsu because it teaches you escapes from pretty much everywhere and most places nowadays will also give you a foundation of wrestling and judo at least where I train does. So the combo I personally train that I really enjoy and think compliments eachother well and gives a good foundation for them training other arts is Muay Thai and BJJ (plus I train balintawak a form of stick fighting and kenjutsu and hema which are two types of historical sword arts one being katana the other longsword and dussack) and those make me feel fairly comfortable in my skills with most weapons and situations but in my opinion variety is an amazing tool so it can’t hurt to at least dabble in many arts 
There’s always something to learn from everyone

text:
The question isn't which one is better in a versus, but which is better suited for a street fight. There are a few things to consider: Kicking above the knee is risky because your balance is more compromised, plus street dudes, not well versed in grappling, still know how to slam someone. 

Also, always assume +1 in any encounter. The last thing you really want to do is get into a grappling situation or even ground fighting (grappling) and their buddy starts stomping you into oblivion. So while grappling is more superior to striking in one on one confrontations (easier to close distance and neutralize strikes than to keep someone at arm's length), it is risky in a true street fight because you likely cannot finish someone with a single clean throw. With striking you have the potential to end it with your first punch. Grappling takes a few steps to get going.

So, out of the styles named, I'd pick boxing (no kicks) or Krav (anything goes mentality), with Muay Thai and Karate (Okinawan) as close seconds. But if I know for sure it's one on one, then all the grappling arts take the top spot, with Wrestling taking a slight lead (teaches you not to be on your back. Head slams into concrete are a possibility with Judo and BJJ ground fighting).

text: Great video sir😂 You know I started out in tma and I have done mma for years now. I love tma but the problem with it lies in the training methods. You need to do strength training, conditioning training and real sparring to make sure your techniques are effective. Tma schools who do this have a far higher succes rate than tma schools who don't. Everything works, and nothing works. It all depends on how you train. Ofcourse there are some techniques that are more effective than others in some ways. Great video!  I was an amateur boxer for a very long time and one of the things that stuck out the most to me was how different boxing gyms could have massively different "feels". My problem with MMA isn't the style, it's the marketing and who they are trying to pull into their doors.

I think what MMA has done is shine a light on techniques that work under pressure and those that don't.
To a point a turning kick is a turning kick and despite subtle differences across various styles they fundementally are the same.

Against most average people a trained traditional martial artist is likely to have an edge in ability and fitness and conditionong but against a trained mma fighter they are apart from some rare exceptions likely to get get taken down and pounded.

Well, strictly personal... MMA(basically Muay Thai, with added wresting) / Muay Thai(Kickboxing with knee and elbow blows), builds up body strength and focus(using simple straightforward techniques ofc) and most importantly, teach people how to take a hard punch or kick anywhere on the body!

While TMA(as you would have it), builds up skill & discipline and offers a larger variety of techniques(some can't be used in a sparring match anyway, as they would severely injure the opponent)... unfortunately most TMA styles, do not offer(or cannot or don't know how to do it) strength, agility and focus training during their workouts... Alas, when met in a real life scenario or face to face with an MMA practitioner, most such cases(over 80 to 90%), come out with a loss for the TMA practitioner! As the TMA practitioner lacks the necessary body strength & agility and is not really used to getting really punched or kicked in the face(or any other place)!

My personal advice??! Start off simple! For example, I started off in Muay Thai & plain Boxing... my very first martial arts ever, although I was initially looking to begin with Northern Shaolin Style, but couldn't find any teachers / schools in my area, I was really "psychic" about Shaolin back in those days! =)) Build up some body strength, agility and focus, learn(get used to it) how to get kicked(take) in the gut(for real), but don't over do it for very long(and don't body build too much either, a little is ok... but if you over do it, it won't help later, with other styles of TMA), or better said, don't "get stuck on it" for too long!

After some 4-5 years of intensive training(at least), which means a minimum of 5 to 6, 90 minute workouts per week, or 6-7 years if you workout only 3 times per week, you can stop and look for a more complex style of Martial Arts... my personal case... stumbled across Wing Chun! Love it! =) Thing is now, I'm not afraid to go one on one, using Wing Chun style with an MMA / Muay Thai practitioner at all... even if I don't win! I just don't care! It's all about fair play and staying friends after the fight! =)

text:
MMA was originally intended as a COMPETITION FORMAT to make possible the confrontation between various fighting specialities (just like how K1 was). I think this is misunderstood today, as many practice MMA as a "martial art" by itself, forgetting that it was originally a format that allowed anybody to use almost whatever technique was in their arsenal. Let's return to the original meaning of MMA: a way of testing and finding out what works, not to exclude any traditional art, rather to better everyone's understanding of what they practice - be it Kickboxing, Muay Thai, Wing Chun, Aikido, you name it. Even in training methods: muscle training is great, tendon training is great too, meditation techniques, breathing techniques - the world is very vast on this matter, and it appeals much more to me to discover those methods rather then criticize them based on the performance in a contest - which depend much more on the person who uses it then on the method itself - when I know nothing of it.
From an evolutionary point of view, it really holds more value - to me - to understand WHY people who went out in war practiced that way, and to take that point to evolve modern fighting, and at the same time re-introduce reality-based sparring mutuated from modern sports in methods that traditionally don't practice that way. 
That's my two cents on the question.

text:
I favor TMA over MMA, though it is also with an eye for aesthetics. MMA comes across as flavorless and bland, whereas TMA have a broader range of personalization, as opposed to MMA, which techniques seem statistics based and tend to follow a cookie cutter model (which is funny considering that is the MMA Perception of TMA).

I've blended different martial arts together, with my primary combination being sabre fencing and Taekwondo. I also implement aspects of things like Uechi Ryu, Aikido, and Sumo (more useful than it sounds) via observation (My technique in any specifically may be well below subpar, but I try to absorb aspects of their principles). Regarding my primary technique, however, I trained specifically in TKD for 20 years (since I was 4 until the day I tore my ACL at around age 24-25). During that period, I also studied Fencing for 7 years (1 year of foil, 6 years of sabre) completely independent from TKD, so those two are the most emphasized styles I blended.

Regarding technique gaps in TMA that seem as if they have no way of countering specific attacks or broader categories like grappling, chances are that the style does actually have counters to them, but are not often taught, which would make sense if the style was used in actual warfare (as it is adapt or perish). What's annoying with TKD (I studied the World Taekwondo Federation style) is that sparring is super wonky, and actually makes practitioners sloppy over time. TKD is often put up as a solely kick focused style, and a lot of that is due to what is seen during sparring (specifically that kicks to the head are legal, but punches to the head are not). The style does actually have a broad range of hand techniques. While I knew the hand techniques, I did not know how to implement them effectively until fencing. I don't punch like a boxer/kickboxer, but rather it is more like a fencing lunge. Rather than a long combination of strikes, I step deep in a manner akin to a lunge as I punch to impale. I actually had to hold it back during sparring as I often got accidental TKO's when training (the opponents crumple and drop for an extended period of time, even if protected by the padded torso protectors). My techniques are all taught in TKD, I just use them in a different manner (I suspect it would superficially resemble Chinese Kempo). I also use techniques that are seen much more often in any of the other aspects of the style, but never used during sparring - specifically the stances. Typically people rely on the fighting stance for everything in sparring, where I learned to flow through each stance as a result of studying fencing footwork. I've actually floored opponents simply through footwork and not even needing to land a hit.

Aside from thickness, which is the same, the boards I trained with were 12x12. The question itself is if you noticed any strange resistance there. I was trying to punch through 4 boards when I was 13-14. I could go through 3 like butter, but adding the 4th I found myself unable to break any of them in fact, the boards actually seemed to bend and flex a bit on impact, literally pushing my hand away. Did you ever run into that problem and if so, what was your solution? I've done 3 with both a regular punch and ox jaw strike (using the wrist bone to strike, in the event you are unfamiliar with the term).

The second question is a phenomenon I noticed while sparring that I can't quite explain, and was wondering if you had any similar experience. I noticed that from those in lower ranks all the way into black belts, opponents will tend to kick and punch at air a foot or two away from my body. I don't dodge, I just stand still and it happens. I am not sure if they are attempting to lead the target or if it is something else. It's happened about 20-30 times for me. There is also a more extreme version where I dodge as an opponent begins a flurry of attacks, stepping forward and slipping behind them. The weird thing is that even when I am behind them (by roughly a meter or more), they continue their flurry in the same direction they started, striking nothing but air 4 or 5 times more. I am curious if you ever had that happen to you. That one has occurred roughly 5 or 6 times. 

My one thought is that I do have a strange phenomenon outside of sparring that seems to occur even during casual conversation. It seems I am unintentionally stealthy for some reason. text: Before MMA and being a student of the Martial Arts in the 80s, I can tell you that there was so much made up, mis-information, and out right lies from TMAs.  Now between thousands of videos of real fights and MMA "the cat is out of the bag" on what works and what doesn't (high percent vs low percent) At this point if a Martial art school doesn't incorporate and address realistic stand up, clinching, and ground work they are being unethical. This includes but not limited to boxing, wrestling, and BJJ. Some TM artist will say "our style is more Art than Martial" but if you poll the students they will say they thought they thought they were learning how to defend them selves. I have witnessed many situations where people have not only wasted years and thousands of dollars, but also could really get themselves hurt if they tried to implement what they were taught in real life situations from TMA training

text: Mixed Martial Arts vs Traditional Martial Arts. It's a debate that been going on for decades over which one is "better". Unfortunately, it would take a whole book to find out which one is "better". I'll attempt to give a short version over which one is "better". If you live in a highly industrialized nation like America, chances are you live in a society filled to the brim with "rules" you must follow. I practice a African martial art called Laamb wrestling. I practice a modified version of Laamb wrestling. I practice for self defense instead of combat glory. The Serer ethnic group was practicing Laamb wrestling for thousands of years. There Laamb wrestling was much more brutal than today Laamb wrestling, so there methods wouldn't work today for any society for the most part. However the people who practice Laamb wrestling today, there methods would go much better even in today's times, so long as it's a contest agreed upon. The same exact thing can be said for "mixed martial arts" vs "traditional martial arts". Would you say poking someone in the eye wouldn't work🤔🤔🤔??? Plenty "traditional martial arts" have such dangerous techniques, while "mix martial arts" hardly have any. Hence why eye poking, strikes to the temple, hits to the bridge of the nose, and other moves that could easily put a human body in jeopardy are banned outright. Even though I can't tell you which martial art you should practice, (that's for you to decide) I can say it'll probably be better to stick with a martial art that best suit you. As a American, and a Sofa Knight,  I'm just giving my take on the martial arts. That's my story. Yera💧.

I lived in China for about two years to train full-time with various teachers. The main issue is the lost of understanding the traditional "meta". Sparring always frames itself arrow a certain meta, the game within the the game of what you are trying to achieve. If you're applying a kickboxing meta, then you'll be trying to get in shots, If its jiu-jistu you'll be trying to get the submission, in judo the throw, in MMA its usually a mix of the kickboxing and the jiu-jistu meta where you switch between getting strikes in and wrestling for submission.

So sparring is only good to train a certain meta, or fighting mentality. The issue is that very few people today can teach you a traditional meta or fighting mentality. Wing Chun for instance can not be applied with a kickboxing meta or jiu-jitsu meta, so if you learn Wing Chun moves but don't learn the meta where those moves are useful then you wont know what your doing in a fight.
Karate for instance is usually actually kickboxing, because the Japanese took the Karate movements from Okinawa but not the Karate meta, they learned the fight meta from the French kickboxing, so the Japanese Karate meta is actually like a bareknuckle Savate meta. Martial arts like Karate and Silat that have their origin in the larger Chinese martial arts culture and originally operate according the the fighting meta of southern Chinese schools (wing chun, white crane, bak mei etc.). The fighting method is based on achieving position and contact before expressing power at short range. This is typical for Chinese martial arts. The meta or mentality is like this: "I want to get a point of balance close to you before hitting you with my whole body force. In order to get close safely, I will use initial attacks, smothering, grasps and deflections in order to get my balance in a place that undermines my attackers balance, then I will strike with my whole body force."
Its hard to put into words, but hopefully the point comes across that there is a certain mentality with Chinese origin martial arts and traditional martial arts in general that you have to learn and develop through diverse methods of training if you want to apply the historical arts. Thank you.

This is actually not even a "traditional martial arts vs modern martial arts" (subjective terms anyways) topic. It's actually quite simple:
1) learning techniques, is in general good for having a basis, but it does not teach you how to fight
2) to learn how to fight you need to test your techniques: know when to use which, when to attack, knowing which techniques will actually work (for you, because it can depend on the technique, but also on the person. Some techniques are more useful than others, but some people can also make some techniques work work super effective, while for others, that same technique simply doensn't work
3) testing techniques is not a matter of, trying the technique on someone else that is cooperating, no, it means: real sparring
4) addionally, to be able to fight, you need to be fit, strength, stamina, being able to give and take hits
5) if you really want to be "the best fighter", you need experience with both standing and ground fighting. This often means that 1 martial art will not be sufficient

The above applies for all martial arts. But some martial arts in general tick more of the boxes than others. But it is still heavily dependend on the school/dojo. There are also (kick)boxing classes for house wives and dads, where they don't spar, etc.
Also, not everyone has the same goals, not everyone wants or needs to be "the best fighter". But of course it is good for martial arts schools to not fake advertise and act like they are making you into "the best fighter", wil they only teach you some techniques without sparring, etc (like I think happens in Kung Fu a lot and in some lesser karate dojo's.

Also a lot of people don't want to work hard and put effort in something. So especially point number 4 they will minimize, but some will even minimize some of the other points. I wouldn’t say they are dying, but every system has something to bring to the table. It just comes down to if the juice is with the squeeze.

A lot of traditional schools have issues introducing sparring because:

1) they are treated like a daycare
2) the clientele is generally not looking  for hard sparring
3) hard sparring can be very dangerous depending on the style and its intent.

The other thing to consider is the benefits of not hard sparring or doing so conservatively:

1) much lower chance of severe injuries like broken bones and TBI
2) able to spend more time on teaching technique and drilling the techniques to a higher proficiency level
3) the training lifespan of the practitioner drastically increases because they have been subjected to less bodily abuse

I think the appropriate training ideology falls somewhere in between the two extremes. 

Sparring / pressure testing time in a low-medium aggressive environment. This gives a chance to apply significantly more dangerous techniques in a training environment, as well as still triggering stress inoculation training. You can still do some hard sparring days here and there, just adjust the sparring parameters. 

Also understanding the likelihood of a positive outcome is much more likely if you train mindset. You could be the baddest boy in the block known by the best martial material, but if you are not mentally prepared for violence or willing to do violence, then you are a gardener in a war.

text:
Hi, thanks for your video.  I started ITF TKD style in 1980, more for exercise, fitness and social activities.  I was taught traditionally by a Korean Master instructor.  The students had all the techniques explained and demonstrated by the instructor at each belt level.  Non-contact free sparring was introduced at green-belt.  The deliberate reason for non-contact sparring was/is rational.  "Do you really want to puposefully want to injure your sparring partner/friend?  It made sense to me then and still does as I'm not a sadistic person.  I love training to push myself to be more flexible and faster.  Everyone has their own physical and mental limits.  Of course, demonstrations are for promotion aspects and acrobatics achieve good audiences.  The performers skills are real but yes practised and choreographed.  TKD will prepare a person in life skills and self-defence.  As you go from white to black belt and beyond you learn new techniques at each stage.  So of the 100's of these, you may only use 3 in a real fight.  In my case it was 2 and 3 respectively.  In both real fights my first technique were a rising block against a) large stick and b) a Dropping fist.    2nd techniqe I used in both were a wrist twist to put my attackers off balance.  The first fight ended there as he was too surprised to continue.  The 2nd fight continued with my attacker trying to get me in a multitude of wrist locks.. my 3rd techniques were releases.  There was a 4th technique but nit TKD.. it was out of sheer boredom that I dug my finger nails into his forearm that led to him stopping his attack on me.  Those were what TKD has given me.  The ability to defend myself without a punch or kick.  After training hard for a long time, time will slow down in  when in a real fight and your decisions on which attack or defence tool to use will come very quickly.  All those technique repititions over the years become hard-wired into your brain and become automatic by your autonomous nervous system.  I believe the Japanese call it Mushin, "no mind".

Explantion for those who need it: taekwondo was not made for sport. It was made for soldiers. Hand techniques are lacking because soldiers have guns in their hands. Below I break down some basic taekwondo techniques and the real world purpose.

First, back fist and knife hands. Neither is a technique you want to be in a position to use; however, if an enemy grabs your barrel these techniques are game over. Letting go of your gun with your forward hand to prepare the strike, you pull your gun and your enemy toward you with your other hand as you strike. Freeing control of your barrel allowing you to perform taekwondo's ultimate move... the trigger pull.

Second, most taekwondo kicks while powerful are niche. Taekwondo is about establishing a standoff range with an enemy. As such the most effective and useful taekwondo combo is a straight front kick into a jumping front kick. If your enemy is in range to grab your weapon when you point it at them do this first. The first kick is to knock your enemy off balance hopefully preventing them from pointing their guns or knives at you, and the second is to deliver damage force. When done right your enemy will be knocked back to a safer distance allowing you to perform taekwondo's ultimate move... the trigger pull.

TLDR; Taekwondo wasn't made for sports or prolonged hand to hand combat. It is for Korean soldiers to use when necessary in warfare. It is far from useless in the real world.

text:
1st kick: Great for a good ole feint and bait if you know your opponent likes to come in after the whiff (see how after the first turn, the opponent tries to capitalize but instead steps into the second oncoming shot?)

2nd kick: Double kick is great for catching your opponent off guard since most kicks are thrown one at a time and require a certain degree of "setup" to pull off. In that same vein, double kicking is fantastic for level changing kicks, as you'll notice the first kick is thrown low, which brings the opponent's attention low, and it does minimal damage, lulling the opponent into a false sense of security, and then the second kick is immediately whipped high at a much higher degree of force

3rd kick: The question mark kick is also a feint and bait type kick, where the initial chambering of the leg draws your opponent's attention low, making him believe you're about to attack his leg or body, and then immediately pivoting and extending to attack his head instead

4th kick: Despite her demonstrating the kick while standing in place (which shows great control on her part by the way), this kick is actually a fantastic way to close large distances while remaining dynamic and posing a threat. I've probably said this a thousand times already, but here goes: a person whose base art is Kyokushin, Boxing, and/or Muay Thai who also crosstrains in Taekwondo is a very very dangerous fighter. And I am saying this as someone who used to hate on Taekwondo so much.

For context: We have a friend back then who is extremely talented and gifted in martial arts and since childhood, he's been doing various forms of martial arts. We simply could not beat him. His first focus was on Shotokan Karate but he gladly crosstrained in other arts like Boxing, Panantukan (Filipino based hand martial arts), Sikaran (similar to Taekwondo), Muay Thai, Judo, and also, Taekwondo.

I tried to spar with him a couple of times, only for me to often be easily beaten by his leg kicks. One time, I thought that perhaps I have already did lots of thigh conditioning and that I could definitely try to catch his legs and start punching on him from there or even do a takedown. But as soon as our sparring started, he gave me a dose of a spinning heel kick and that spinning heel kick honestly hurts way more than his typical attacks coming from his shin. From there, it was what made me change my perception of Taekwondo. Because not only is he flexible, but he is extremely agile on his feet and he could easily switch to and from one stance to another, something that is being taught in TKD. 

Personally, I haven't tried training in Taekwondo but I do plan to soon. I did training in Kyokushin Karate and Muay Thai and I used to often disregard or not take spinning kicks seriously, thinking that they're too predictable. But many times, I often get caught by a well timed spinning back and side kick. So from there, I decided to finally include TKD moves into my arsenal. But I would still love to formally train in Taekwondo so that I could practice their kicks more safely, for better discipline, and for someone to actually correct my forms if ever. And of course, to have fun and socialize.

text: Tae Kwon Do criticism for me is challenging, because the place I trained at for ~7 years was phenomenal. The instructor was a world class expert in TKD, Penkat Silat, Aikido, and Jujitsu. So, I have to admit, I'm not entirely sure if my TKD experience is representative of all TKD clubs. I think the biggest problem -- which was mentioned in the video -- is that there are so many McDojongs in TKD that it gets a bad wrap. The criticisms are strange to me (again, could be my specific club), but I've never heard that their kicks are weak. In my club, the higher ranks could absolutely fold someone in half with a simple roundhouse. Their spinning backkicks were downright terrifying. Also, those demos with 720 deg kicks really aren't the norm. Those are specifically trained competition/demo athletes. I'm in karate now (Isshin Ryu), and while different, I learned just as much with hands in my TKD class. I don't think TKD is a full marital art and definitely has some holes; but the most important part I learned was footwork, balance, speed, and accuracy, and that translates well to fighting, whether in a tournament or on the street. It's fantastic for learning striking of all kinds (including knees and elbows); its biggest hole is a complete lack of grappling.

Good break down. No doubt TKD suffers from its popularity and sports rules. Another thing I think TKD fighters are great at is SOME aspects of distance management. Their capacity to lure opponents with their leg and stance switch and then break the distance in an instant is remarkable. Related to that also is their habit to counter/angle off and strike back in the same moment. Now when the distance gets too close of course, they can be clueless and easy to punch, sweep or take down.

In the early 90s, in europe, while training wushu sanshu / sanda, we had taekwondo cats coming to cross-train and go on tournaments with us in order to compete in a different set of rules (sweeps, take down, no head and chest gear, this was before Sanda rules had spread to europe). My instructor also trained in TKD and we integrated many of their kick training routines. These cats were so quick and powerful, we’d trade kicking technics for sweeps and take down one. But well they didn’t come out of mc dojos in strip malls but rather good old martial arts club in the hood, that makes a big difference on the intent. I barely recognize TKD nowadays when looking at what the sport has become. I still love the style though, it offers many great resources and strategies in my opinion.

Like it or not, the TKD instructor (unless he has income from elsewhere) is a businessman first, and a martial arts instructor second. He needs to be able to support himself and his family financially. That means attracting the most students as possible, and that means making the TKD school a place that attracts people of all ages, ability, etc. This is just the reality of it.

And yes, TKD guys can kick very hard. To say TKD is useless because Muay Thai students can kick harder misses a fundamental point. And that is there is only so much power one needs to knock someone out or break bones. This reminds me of in school how kids would say, 'I have a 9 mm" and the other kid says, "yeah, well I have a 45" but the point is both are deadly and it doesn't matter if one is more powerful than the other, you won't survive either one.

As for TKD sparring. TKD is trying to be a sport as much as a martial art. It's not as if the leaders of the leading TKD organizations don't realize that in real fights there is a lot of punching to the face or grabs/grappling/clinching. Of course they know that. But they are trying to make it a sport and aren't worried about practical fighting, anymore than boxers are worried that their sport isn't effective in a real fight. And the reason for what seems like ridiculous rules in Olympic TKD (no punching to the face, no leg kicks, etc) is because they're trying to make it unique sport, one that is and LOOKS different than kickboxing.

if someone wants to learn to actually fight, TKD in general isn't the place for you. And I can't blame them, if I were a TKD instructor, I wouldn't gear it towards fighters either, as that's not where the money is. So I say, join TKD but know you're doing it for similar reasons someone joins cardio kickboxing or joins boxing. To get in shape and have fun or because you like the unique sport of TKD.

Hi Rob, thank you for this analysis. I practice taekwondo (tkd) and I would like to add some comments to what you said. There are 3 types of tkd: WT taekwondo, the Olympic style, ITF taekwondo the traditional style and the style I practice, and the ATA, the American version of taekwondo, which alas, I know very little about. When it comes to power, during ITF competitions there is a session called power breaking during which the participants have to break special plastic boards that are about 1 inch thick and for adults black belts the boards are two. You need to break these boards using hands and/or kicks. These boards are designed to break only if you strike with the right amount of power (a lot of it!) and on precise spots. There are many videos on YouTube if you want to have a look at it (just type in ITF breaking competitions). Lastly, hands, in ITF tkd we use punches a lot. This style, in fact, is very similar to kick boxing (not very similar though) alternating hands and kicks.
So as you can see tkd (especially the ITF) it's not too watered down since it is highly regulated (at least here in Europe) and if you do not meet the standards for a black belt you simply fail your grading (usually panels have external examiners).

Hands are used a lot in ITF, not as much as muay-thai, but still a lot!

text:
I'm an ITF Taekwon-do black belt (3rd dan) from Europe. TKD was originally intended to destroy or break your opponent with a single well placed attack with the right "weapon" on a weak point to your opponent's body. Like a knife hand thrust to the throat or an elbow to the solar plexus.

Ice cold showers and conditioning/hardening of your fists, forearms, legs and shins is mandatory if you practice by the book. Original TKD comes from Kyokushin Karate and was thought to the Korean military as a last resort. It was feared by the Vietcong.

text:
I wholeheartedly agree that many traditional martial arts paths have become diluted over time. The numbers themselves are telling. World Taekwondo (WT), one of the sport's largest governing bodies, reports approximately 80 million practitioners globally, while another source, the World Taekwondo Organization (WTO), claims that number exceeds 200 million. We must question if there are truly that many qualified teachers to support such a massive number of students. If not, this presents the first major issue.

Investing in a black belt can be a significant financial commitment, often costing ten thousand dollars or more. Much like buying a new car or a house, this isn't a decision you should make based on convenience, such as the studio's schedule or proximity to your home. You are paying for a teacher, and that instructor should be focused on teaching, not on profiting excessively from hidden fees and high student turnover, which can often be signs of a flawed ideology.

This leads to a crucial distinction: self-defense and fighting are not the same.

Gichin Funakoshi, the founder of modern Shotokan karate, believed the ultimate goal of karate was to improve a practitioner's character, not simply to prepare for physical combat. His philosophy centered on the idea that training should instill virtues like respect, discipline, and humility to create better individuals.

In contrast, Mixed Martial Arts (MMA) training is designed to prepare a fighter for a real, unpredictable combat scenario. This involves full-contact sparring, where techniques are tested against a resisting opponent. Many traditional martial arts, however, often emphasize forms (katas) and pre-arranged drills with limited or no full-contact sparring. This difference in training can leave practitioners unprepared for the chaos and pressure of an actual fight.

MMA also values versatility. A fighter specializing in a single discipline, like boxing, may be an expert at punching but is vulnerable to takedowns and grappling. Conversely, a fighter who only practices a grappling art like Judo might excel at throws but be at a disadvantage against a skilled striker. MMA forces fighters to be proficient in all ranges of combat—standing, in the clinch, and on the ground—making them more adaptable to any situation.

The goal of karate is self-defense, not necessarily to fight a trained opponent. We can explore extremes to illustrate this point: could a 90-pound girl with a decade of MMA experience stop a prime Mike Tyson from taking her purse? At some point, the answer is no. MMA, which has evolved during my lifetime (I was born in 1967), is simply mixed martial arts, and I understand the arguments well.

Not everyone is a twenty or thirty-year-old in peak physical condition who can survive a full-on MMA fight; even many of those who compete don't do well. I started with Tae Kwon Do before moving to Tang Soo Do, but the two-hour commute from my country home made it unsustainable. I later joined an MMA gym opened by a local Alabama fighter not far from my job. I fought four times and quickly discovered it wasn't for me.

After that, I worked with a private trainer, moved back here, and then hired another private trainer before finally committing to a studio to earn my black belt. I wanted to achieve it before I was too old and finally settled in one place long enough to complete the journey. I've also studied boxing and kickboxing, as well as Japanese sword, though not in the most traditional sense.

I took Kenpo from a former world champion and hall-of-fame member and found that the program for earning a black belt was different from the program for sparring and competing. In my opinion, the belt curriculum, which was devised by the Traceys based on Ed Parker’s work with some tweaks, differed greatly from the fighting and sparring curriculum designed by Joe Lewis, a legendary martial artist and kickboxer.

Lewis developed a fighting system based on 25 principles he believed were crucial for success in combat. These principles are rooted in efficiency, strategy, and a blend of mental and physical preparation.

Setups: Confusing an opponent physically and mentally by practicing timing, distance, and using misleading body language.

Positioning: Maintaining a relaxed state for explosive power while staying assertive to control the fight.

Independent Movement: A strike should move independently of the body to eliminate "leading centers" and make movements more deceptive.

Initial Speed: The ability to relax and explode into action, which is more important than overall speed.

Critical Distance Line: Understanding the opponent's effective range to position yourself defensively and offensively.

Line of Attack: The three primary routes to a target: inside, outside, and middle.

Bridging the Gap: Effectively closing the distance using initial speed and proper footwork.

Five Primary Techniques: Lewis’s core techniques: the sidefist/backfist, inverted close punch, reverse punch, side kick/roundhouse kick, and spinning rear kick.

Leading Side vs. Rear Side: Using techniques from the leading side for greater economy of motion and speed.

Economy of Motion: Prioritizing the most direct, straight-line route to the target.

Relaxation vs. Tension: Relaxation is key to speed and energy conservation, while tension slows you down and makes you predictable.

Mobility vs. Immobility: Using various footwork techniques to create unpredictability.

Extension, Hyperextension, Double Hyperextension: Increasing your reach to extend your own critical distance line.

Leading Centers: Eliminating tell-tale movements that give away your next move, or using them intentionally for faking.

Unpredictability vs. Classical Form: The importance of not being predictable by varying rhythm, angle, and using feints.

Straight Line vs. Curved Line: The straight line is the most direct and powerful route to a target.

Body Rhythm vs. Broken Rhythm: Using fluid, continuous motion versus interrupted, unpredictable motion to disorient an opponent.

The Three-Point Principle: Keeping three points of the body stable for readiness to attack or defend.

Forward Pressure: Continuously moving forward to overwhelm an opponent psychologically and physically.

Half-Commitment vs. Full-Commitment vs. Extension-Commitment: Committing to a strike with different degrees of force and follow-through.

Attack by Combination: Using a combination of strikes to overwhelm defenses.

Attack by Interception: Attacking an opponent as they are attacking you to neutralize their offense.

Feinting: Using deceptive movements to create an opening.

Deception and Faking: Using a range of misleading actions to trick an opponent into making a mistake.

The Law of the Lead Hand and Foot: The leading hand and foot should be the primary tools for probing, controlling distance, and initiating attacks.Today at 58 I am a Shotokan student and hope to get a black belt here as well before I get to old

I did karate for a year or so. Never really got into it. Im in muay thai now and I definitely see a lot of flaws with karate. The blocking first of all is terrible, if you block a jab with a traditional block in karate, it leaves you open for a hook that a quick muay thai fighter will have no challenge landing. Secondly the kicking in karate is actually pretty lame. The reason is because when they kick, they immediately snap there legs back. Basically the kick lands with the shin bone but immediately gets pulled away. And not only that, but there isnt much power in karate kicks because they dont really use their hips. They just kinda throw there leg out there, and immediately snap it back as soon as their kick touches their opponent.

In muay thai, you use your hips to land a completely disabling kick to the body or the head or leg. When you kick in muay thai, you dont immediately snap back your leg. You drive your leg through your opponent basically imagining that you are trying to cut them in half. Not only that but the power comes from the hips, you arent just extending your leg and immediately bringing it back like karate.

I also think the conditioning in general in muay thai is way more significant than what i experienced in karate.

So yeah, my conclusion is that a muay thai fighter would absolutely cripple a karate fighter, or a taekwondo fighter.

text:
as basic information, Tae Kwondo is divided into 2 streams, namely the first ITF and the second WTF - Kukkiwon.. ITF is the origin of the original flow of Tae Kwondo.. But Te Kwondo is actually Korean Karate which is called Tang Soo Do and combined with martial arts that developed in Korea both from Japanese and traditional influences as well as Chinese martial arts, such as Taekkyeon, Soo Bhak Do, Hapkido, Hwa Rang Do, Kuk Sul Won and so on which were then united and nationalized in 1950 by General Choi Hon Hi under the ITF. which later developed into KTA and WTF in the 1970s.. you need to know Tae Kwondo itself is a development of Tang Soo Do -Korean Karate in which practitioners, instructors and students are Korean citizens who study in Japan. and Tang Soo Do - Tae Kwondo is actually a Shotokan Karate style. So it's no wonder there are many similarities in Movement in Tul, Poomsae, Tae Geuk, Hyeong, Dongjak/Basic between Tae Kwondo and Tang Soo Do with Karate especially Shotokan.. 
these are the 9 Kwans which pioneer of Tae Kwondo.

Song Moo Kwan(송무관) - first of the original kwans, founded in Kaesong on March 20,1944 by Ro Byung Jik(노병직), who had studied karate under Gichin Funakoshi along with Chung Do Kwan founder Lee Won Kuk in Japan.

Chung Do Kwan(청도관) - second kwan dojang in Korea founded in September, 1944 by Lee Won Kuk(이원국). He studied Taekkyeon in Seoul, He also studied Shotokan Karate in Japan, Kung Fu in Henan and Shanghai in China, and other.[

Moo Duk Kwan(무덕관) - was founded in 1945 by Hwang Kee(황기) teaching Hwa Soo Do. Hwang studied Taekkyon, T'ai chi and some types of Kung Fu in China. His first two attempts at running a school of Hwa Soo Do were unsuccessful. After 1946, realizing that most Koreans were unfamiliar with the Chinese-based arts he was teaching, he incorporated the more familiar, Japanese influenced, Tang Soo Do into his curriculum. By 1953 and onward until 1960, the Moo Duk Kwan had risen to become biggest martial arts organization in Korea, with close to 75% of all martial artists in Korea practicing Tang Soo Do Moo Duk Kwan. In 1957, Hwang made a discovery of Soo Bahk(수박), a traditional Korean martial art from Muyedobotongji(무예도보통지). In 1960, the Korean Soo Bahk Do (수박도) Association was incorporated and officially registered with the Korean government as the traditional Korean martial art. The following year, the Moo Duk Kwan Soo Bahk Do discipline was recognized internationally for the first time.

Ji Do Kwan(지도관) - Chosun Yun Mu Kwan Kong Soo Do Club (조선연무관 공수도부, Chosun Yun Mu Kwan had been the original Japanese Kodokan Judo school in Korea for over 30 years previously) founded March 3, 1946 by Chun Sang Sup(전상섭), who had studied Shotokan karate with Gichin Funakoshi in Japan, and later called his art 'Kong Soo Do(공수도)'. He had a very close relationship with Yoon Byung-In, founder of YMCA Kwon Bop Club. Chun and Yoon would travel to train with other martial artists, sometimes traveling to Manchuria. They trained with each other so much that they became known as brothers. Chun went missing during the Korean War; subsequently, this kwan voted to change its name to 'Jidokwan'. After Chun disappeared in Korean War, the original students of Chun voted Master Yoon Kwe-byung(윤쾌병, Trained Chuan Fa in Manchuria) as Jidokwan 1st President.

Chang Moo Kwan(창무관) - YMCA Kwon Bop Club(YMCA 권법부) founded in 1946 by Yoon Byung-in(윤병인), who had studied Chinese Kung Fu (Quan fa). When he studied in Nihon University, he trained Shudokan karate under grandmaster Kanken Tōyama.[ Unlike other taekwondo kwans, early Chang Moo Kwan was mainly based on Chinese Kung Fu (Quan-fa). The early Chang Moo Kwan taught Palgi kwon(팔기권) (which influenced by Bajiquan).[ Yoon went missing during the Korean War. His teachings were carried on by his top student Lee Nam Suk, who changed the name of the school to Chang Moo Kwan. 10th Dan Grandmaster Soon Bae Kim is one of two Kukkiwon 10th Dans in charge of Kukkiwon testing.

Han Moo Kwan(한무관) - founded in August 1954 by Lee Kyo Yoon as an offshoot of the Yun Moo Kwan/Jidokwan. 

Oh Do Kwan(오도관) - founded in 1955 by Choi Hong Hi, who also became honorary head of the Chung Do Kwan. Top instructors were Nam Tae Hi and Han Cha Kyo.

Kang Duk Won(강덕원) - founded in 1956 by Park Chul Hee and Hong Jong Pyo as an offshoot of the Kwon Bop Bu/Chang Moo Kwan.

Jung Do Kwan(정도관) - founded in 1956 by Lee Yong Woo (died August, 2006) as an offshoot of the Chung Do Kwan.

The Kwans united in 1955 as Tae Soo Do. In the beginning of 1957, the name Taekwondo was adopted by several Korean martial arts masters, for its similarity to the name Tae Kyon.

General Choi established ITF-Taekwondo (which practices a   more traditional form of taekwondo) while WTF-Taekwondo   (which has a strong emphasis on sparring) became an Olympic sport in 2000.

A goodwill trip to North-Korea in 1966 caused General Choi to fall in disgrace in the eyes of the South-Koreans. Choi resigned as president of the K.T.A. and founded the I.T.F. on March, the   22nd of that same year. The headquarters of ITF was established in Canada.

ITF started concentrating on the forms developed by General   Choi, while the KTA (which later, on May 28, 1973, became the WTF) concentrated on the Palgwe’s. Later the WTF abandoned the Palgwe’s and started concentrating on Taeguks. Slowly, the WTF emphasis turned to sparring. This is also the reason why a lot of people call (WTF) Taekwondo a ‘Martial Sport’ rather than a ‘Martial Art’.

text:
I started as a kid with shotokan karate but I had a terrible teacher which made me drop martial arts for around 22 years. Then I picked up boxing and fell in love with it, while adding taekwondo to work on my legs some more. Taekwondo is a bit too similar to karate for my taste, but the difference is clear- keeping distance, looking for openings and delivering precise strikes. You chamber kicks to make the opponent guess which kick you perform, to fake kicks or to just kick again. It requires a ton of balance and speed compared to karate. It's pretty negligent on hands but it's not an issue for a boxer, since boxing strikes make karate ones look like jokes anyway.

Karate is more balanced than taekwondo when it comes to using hands and feet, there is a lot of focus on front-back movement while being well balanced in order to get more power. When it comes to styles of boxing- taekwondo is like outboxing while karate is like inboxing, both require a lot of movement but in a very different way.

All that being said- when it comes to the "art" of "martial arts" both aint got shit on northern kung fu styles. These are some of the most beautiful movements a human body can perform

While Karate offers a balanced split of hands and feet, Taekwondo relies about 70% on kicking.Key DifferencesOrigin: Karate originated in Okinawa, Japan, rooted in traditional Zen philosophy. Taekwondo was developed in Korea, emphasizing dynamic movement and modern athleticism.Technique: Karate focuses on a balanced mix of punches, elbows, and kicks, with rigid stances to deliver maximum power. Taekwondo heavily emphasizes agility, flexibility, and dynamic footwork.Competitions: Karate tournaments often involve kata (forms) and kumite (point/continuous sparring). Taekwondo is an Olympic sport governed by World Taekwondo (WT) or the International Taekwondo Federation (ITF), emphasizing dynamic, fast-paced sparring.Self-Defense: Karate provides a more versatile approach to close-range combat. Taekwondo teaches students to maintain distance using rapid kicking.Which Should You Choose?Choose Karate if: You want a well-rounded, full-body workout that balances punches and kicks, and you appreciate traditional, foundational discipline.Choose Taekwondo if: You love flashy, high-impact kicks, want to develop explosive leg strength, or are interested in Olympic-style competitive sparring.

There´s absolutely no challenge for me in going to a bar and pick a fight with a sad slob who has probably never learn how to defend himself. text: Their description isn't at all like the TKD I learned and got my black belt in. We do use a lot of kicks because they have longer reach and our legs tend to be stronger than our arms. This video seems to be focusing on the "point sport" of TKD rather than as a martial art or form of self-defense. This is the problem with turning anything into a sport. The kicks look cool, so tournaments make them the only way to score points. But there's no point system in real sparring, at least not in the school I was in 25 years ago.  We put on pads and we fought.  If someone was getting pummeled or got hit really hard, our sensei would call "break" and give that person some advice and a moment to recover. text:
While it is a historical fact that Taekwondo was influenced by Karate, it cannot be dismissed as a mere "derivative" or "copycat" martial art. This is because Taekwondo has evolved in a completely different direction in terms of technical principles, body mechanics, and core philosophy.
​Although Taekwondo may have adopted a formal motif from Karate, it has completely overhauled the "engine" (the principles of power generation), the exterior (kicking techniques), and the "driving style" (competition rules) to align with the dynamic spirit of the Korean people.
​The fact that modern Karate is now adopting Taekwondo’s signature techniques is the most definitive evidence that Taekwondo has moved far beyond Karate’s sphere of influence, establishing its own unique "martial superiority."

The Evolution of Taekwondo: From Influence to Innovation and Karate’s Adoption
​Creation of Multi-dimensional and Spinning Kicks:
While Karate kicks were traditionally single-strike attacks from a grounded stance, Taekwondo opened a new dimension by combining weight shifting with aerial maneuvers. Techniques like the Narae-chagi (Double Kick)—delivering multiple strikes in mid-air—and the 360-degree Spinning Kicks are original assets of Taekwondo. Today, elite WKF (World Karate Federation) athletes actively adopt and practice these Taekwondo-style mechanics to score high points in competition.

​Establishment of the Unique 'Bounce Step':
Taekwondo perfected the 'Bounce Step,' a rhythmic, light-footed movement used to control distance and timing, similar to fencing. This is a complete departure from the static stances of traditional Karate. Modern Karate sparring (Kumite) now frequently features practitioners using these light, Taekwondo-style steps to find angles, proving that Karate has integrated Taekwondo's superior footwork for modern sport.
​Shift in Striking Paradigm via Body Protectors (Hogu):
The introduction of body protectors in the early 1960s evolved Taekwondo from a 'stop-impact' art into a 'full-impact' combat sport. This environment allowed for the development of bolder, more explosive techniques. The sheer power and speed of these full-contact kicks established a unique identity for Taekwondo that has now become a benchmark for kicking excellence worldwide.

text:
Etymology - 

Kalaripayattu is a martial art which developed out of combat-techniques of the 11th-12th century battlefield, with weapons and combative techniques that are unique to Kerala. The word Kalaripayattu is a combination of two Malayalam words - kalari (training ground or battleground) and payattu (training of martial arts), which is roughly translated as "practice in the arts of the battlefield".

History -

According to legend, Parashurama, the sixth avatar of Vishnu, learned the art from Shiva, and taught it to the original settlers of Kerala shortly after bringing Kerala up from the ocean floor.[note 1] A song in Malayalam refers to Parashurama's creation of Kerala, and credits him with the establishment of the first 108 kalaris throughout Kerala, along with the instruction of the first 21 Kalaripayattu gurus in Kerala on the destruction of enemies.[5]

According to another legend, Ayyappa, a war deity from Kerala, learned Kalaripayattu in the Cheerappanchira Kalari in Muhamma.
